title: Waves: why shaking faster makes the waves closer together

summary.text: Tap a tray of water twice each second and the ripples sit far apart. Tap four times each second and the ripples squeeze to about half the gap, yet they race across the tray just as fast as before. A pendulum does something just as odd: swing it wide or swing it narrow, and it takes the same time. Your child counts swings, taps ripples and works out a rule with three parts. The hand that starts a wave sets how often the waves come, which scientists call the frequency. What the wave travels through sets how fast it goes. The spacing between crests follows from those two. The same rule holds for sound, radio, light and ripples in space itself. In 1967 a student named Jocelyn Bell found a steady beat coming from the sky, and it turned out to be a star spinning.
summary.art: A steel tray of water with two sets of ripples: wide-spaced rings on the left from slow taps, and close-spaced rings on the right from fast taps, with a small washer pendulum hanging above and a star with a beam in the night sky behind.

intro.hook: Tie a washer to a thread and let it swing. Now pull it back much further and let it swing again. Does the wide swing take longer, or the same time? Most people say longer. Count the swings and find out.
intro.text: The wide swing takes the same time as the narrow one. A pendulum keeps its own beat, and only its length changes it. The same idea sits inside every wave. Whatever starts a wave sets how often the waves come. What the wave travels through sets how fast it goes. Put the two together and you can predict how far apart the crests will be. In this unit you count swings, tap ripples in a tray, and follow the rule from a bucket of water all the way out to radio, light and the stars.
intro.art: A child holding a stopwatch beside a washer on a thread swinging in front of a door frame, with a faint dotted arc showing a wide swing and a narrow swing taking the same time.

outcomes: I can say what frequency is, count it in swings, taps or beats each second, and name the unit, hertz.
I can show with a pendulum that its length changes how often it swings, but its weight and how wide it swings do not.
I can explain that the source of a wave sets how often the waves come, and what the wave travels through sets how fast it goes.
I can use the tap rate and the wave speed to work out the wavelength, and check my answer with ripples.
I can tell a push wave from a shake wave and say which kind sound and earthquake waves are.
I can say what amplitude tells us about a wave's energy, and why ripples shrink as they spread.
I can place ripples, sound, radio and light by wavelength, and tell how Jocelyn Bell found a steady beat from a star.

terms.meaning: How many times something repeats in one second. For a wave, it is how many crests pass a spot each second.
terms.example: A resting child's heart beats about once and a half each second, so its frequency is about one and a half beats each second.
terms.art: A child with two fingers on her wrist and a clock showing one second, with small heart-beat marks beside it.

terms.meaning: The unit for frequency. One hertz means once each second. Write it Hz.
terms.example: A clock that ticks once a second ticks at 1 hertz. A ceiling light on the mains in India flickers 100 times a second, from a supply of 50 hertz.
terms.art: A wall clock with a tick mark and a label that says 1 hertz.

terms.meaning: The time one full swing or one full wave takes. It is the opposite way of saying frequency.
terms.example: A pendulum that makes 1 swing every 2 seconds has a period of 2 seconds. Its frequency is half a swing each second.
terms.art: A pendulum drawn at three moments with a bracket labelled 2 seconds under the whole there-and-back swing.

terms.meaning: Any weight hanging from a string or rod that swings to and fro.
terms.example: A child's swing, a hanging lamp and the weight inside an old wall clock are all pendulums.
terms.art: A playground swing, a hanging lamp and an old wall clock with a swinging weight, side by side.

terms.meaning: A pendulum going from one side across to the other side and all the way back to where it began.
terms.example: Let go of a washer on the left. When it comes back to the left again, that is one swing.
terms.art: A washer on a thread with arrows showing it going right and then back left to the start.

terms.meaning: The thing that starts a wave by moving back and forth.
terms.example: Your tapping finger is the source of the ripples. A guitar string is the source of a guitar sound.
terms.art: A finger tapping a tray of water with rings spreading out from the point.

terms.meaning: The distance from one crest of a wave to the next crest. It is also how far one wave travels while the source makes one full beat.
terms.example: Ripples from slow taps in a tray can be 14 centimetres apart. Ripples from fast taps can be 7 centimetres apart.
terms.art: A wavy line with a double arrow between two neighbouring crests and a ruler under it.

terms.meaning: How far a wave travels in one second. It is set by what the wave travels through.
terms.example: Ripples in 1 centimetre of water travel about 30 centimetres each second. Sound in air travels about 340 metres each second.
terms.art: A ripple crest at the start and again one second later, with a measuring tape showing how far it went.

terms.meaning: How far a wave rises above its flat resting level. A bigger amplitude means more energy in the wave.
terms.example: A gentle ripple has an amplitude of a few millimetres. A storm wave at sea can have an amplitude of several metres.
terms.art: Two waves, one low and one tall, each with an arrow from the flat line up to the crest.

terms.meaning: A wave in which the material is pushed together and pulled apart along the direction the wave travels. Scientists call it a longitudinal wave.
terms.example: A squeeze that runs along a spring toy is a push wave. Sound in air is a push wave too.
terms.art: A spring toy with a squeezed group of coils moving right and arrows along the spring.

terms.meaning: A wave in which the material moves across the direction the wave travels. Scientists call it a transverse wave.
terms.example: A bump that runs along a dupatta is a shake wave. The cloth moves up and down while the bump goes sideways.
terms.art: A dupatta with a bump and arrows showing the cloth moving up and down while the bump moves along.

terms.meaning: The rate at which something likes to swing or shake when you leave it alone. Scientists call it the natural frequency.
terms.example: A pendulum 1 metre long has a natural beat of one swing every 2 seconds, however you start it.
terms.art: A long pendulum and a short pendulum side by side with a slow beat label and a fast beat label.

terms.meaning: What happens when pushes arrive at the same beat as the natural beat of the thing being pushed. Each small push adds to the swing, so it grows big.
terms.example: You push a friend on a swing at the moment the swing comes back to you. Small pushes at the right time make a big swing.
terms.art: A girl on a playground swing and a parent pushing at the top of each swing, with the swing getting higher in three pictures.

terms.meaning: The energy a wave carries from its source to wherever it ends. A taller wave carries more.
terms.example: A big sea wave can knock you over. A tiny ripple only tickles your toes.
terms.art: A tall wave knocking over a sandcastle and a tiny ripple touching a toe.

terms.meaning: Light is a wave that needs no material to travel through. Its wavelength decides its colour.
terms.example: Red light has longer waves than violet light. About a hundred waves of red light would fit across the width of one hair.
terms.art: A rainbow with a long wave drawn under the red end and a short wave drawn under the violet end.

terms.meaning: A wave like light, but with a much longer wavelength, used to carry radio, television and phone signals.
terms.example: An FM radio station at 100 megahertz sends waves about 3 metres long. Your Wi-Fi sends waves about 12 centimetres long.
terms.art: A radio tower sending long waves towards a house with a radio and a Wi-Fi box.

terms.meaning: A very small length. There are a billion nanometres in one metre.
terms.example: Light waves are between about 400 and 700 nanometres long.
terms.art: A metre stick, then a hair, then a tiny wave, each zoomed in more, with a label of nanometres.

terms.meaning: A spinning star that sends out a beam of radio waves, like a lighthouse. Each time the beam sweeps past Earth, we receive a pulse.
terms.example: The first pulsar found sent a pulse every 1.3 seconds, as steady as a clock.
terms.art: A small bright star with two beams sweeping round like a lighthouse, and a distant radio telescope receiving pulses.

explanations.context: This card says what frequency is, using swings you can count.
explanations.definition: Frequency is how many times something repeats in one second. It is counted in hertz. One hertz is once each second.
explanations.description: Watch a washer on a thread. Count ten swings and time them. If ten swings take 10 seconds, the washer makes 1 swing each second, so its frequency is 1 hertz. If ten swings take 20 seconds, the washer makes half a swing each second, which is half a hertz. Things around you have frequencies too. A resting child's heart beats about 80 to 100 times each minute, which is about one and a half hertz. A hummingbird beats her wings around 50 times each second. A tune on a violin string can shake 440 times each second. The wave comes from a source that repeats, and each repeat sends out one more crest.
examples: A wall clock ticks once each second, so it ticks at 1 hertz.
A hummingbird's wings beat around 50 times each second, so her wing frequency is around 50 hertz.
The mains electricity in an Indian home swings back and forth 50 times each second, a frequency of 50 hertz.
explanations.art: Three rows of tick marks: a slow row for a clock, a medium row for a heart, and a very fast row for a hummingbird, each with a hertz label.

explanations.concept: Period: the time for one swing
explanations.context: This card gives the other way to say how often, the time for one swing.
explanations.definition: The period is the time one full swing or one full wave takes. The frequency is how many fit in one second. If the period is 2 seconds, the frequency is half a hertz.
explanations.description: There are two ways to say the same thing. You can say how many swings fit in one second, or how long one swing takes. A fast pendulum makes many swings in a second, and each one takes a short time. A slow pendulum makes few swings, and each one takes a long time. The two numbers are partners. If one swing takes 0.5 seconds, 2 swings fit in each second. If one swing takes 4 seconds, a quarter of a swing fits in each second. A short period and a high frequency always go together.
examples: A pendulum that swings once every 2 seconds has a period of 2 seconds and a frequency of half a hertz.
A hummingbird wing that beats 50 times each second takes one fiftieth of a second for each beat.
A sea wave that arrives every 8 seconds has a period of 8 seconds, so less than one wave arrives each second.
explanations.art: A pendulum with a stopwatch showing 2 seconds beside a ruler of one-second slots with only half a swing in the slot.

explanations.concept: What sets the beat of a pendulum
explanations.context: This card explains what you found in the Counting Swings test: length matters, weight and width do not.
explanations.definition: The time a pendulum takes for one swing depends on its length. It does not depend on the weight of the bob, and for small swings it does not depend on how wide the swing is.
explanations.description: In the Counting Swings test, a 25 centimetre pendulum swung once in about 1 second. A 100 centimetre pendulum swung once in about 2 seconds. So the string became four times as long, and the time for one swing became twice as long. A heavier washer did not change the time. A wider swing did not change it either. A wide swing has further to go, but it is also pulled back harder at the start, so it moves faster, and the two effects cancel for small swings. Galileo is reported to have noticed this about 1583 by watching a hanging lamp in a church in Pisa, and he later wrote about pendulums with a lead ball and a cork ball that swung together. For very wide swings, the time does grow a little.
examples: A very long pendulum, such as a swing hung from a tall tree branch, swings slowly.
A short pendulum, such as a washer on a 25 centimetre thread, swings once each second.
A child on a swing takes the same time per swing whether her friend pushes gently or hard, as long as the swing stays in the same ropes.
explanations.art: A long pendulum with a slow beat label and a short pendulum with a fast beat label, plus a heavy washer and a light paper clip on equal threads swinging together.

explanations.concept: The source sets how often, and the material sets how fast
explanations.context: This card joins the Tray Test from Class 3 with what you found about frequency.
explanations.definition: The source of a wave sets the frequency, which is how often crests are made. The material the wave travels through sets the wave speed. These are two separate settings.
explanations.description: Think of a person standing by a road throwing a ball to a friend every 2 seconds. How often a ball leaves is the thrower's choice. How fast each ball flies is decided by the throw and the air. A wave is a little different, because the wave speed is not up to the source at all. It is set by the material. When you tap a tray of water twice each second, two crests leave each second. They travel at the speed that water of that depth allows. If you tap faster, more crests leave each second, but each one still travels at the same speed. So the crests end up closer together. Nothing about the tapping changed the speed. Only the number of crests per second changed.
examples: A finger tapping a tray twice each second makes two crests every second. Each travels at the speed of the water.
Plucking a guitar string harder makes the sound louder but not higher, because the string sets how often it shakes.
A crowd Mexican wave goes at the speed of the people in it, however fast the first person stands.
explanations.art: A hand at the left end of a tray making two crests every second, with an arrow marked speed set by the water along the tray.

explanations.concept: Wavelength comes from speed and frequency
explanations.context: This card gives the rule that joins frequency, wave speed and wavelength, which you test with ripples.
explanations.definition: The wavelength is how far a wave travels during one beat of the source. So wavelength equals wave speed divided by frequency. Also, wave speed equals frequency times wavelength.
explanations.description: Suppose ripples travel 30 centimetres each second. Tap once each second. By the time the next tap happens, the first crest has gone 30 centimetres. So the crests are 30 centimetres apart. Tap twice each second. Now one tap happens every half second, and the first crest has gone only 15 centimetres. So the crests are 15 centimetres apart. Tap four times each second, and the crests are 7.5 centimetres apart. Faster taps make shorter wavelengths. You can also read the rule the other way. If you measure the wavelength and you know the frequency, multiply them, and you get the speed. 4 taps each second times 7.5 centimetres is 30 centimetres each second.
examples: A sound of 340 hertz in air, which travels about 340 metres each second, has a wavelength of about 1 metre.
A sound of 1,000 hertz has a wavelength of about 34 centimetres, because 340 divided by 1,000 is 0.34 metres.
Ripples that travel 30 centimetres each second and are made 3 times each second are 10 centimetres apart.
explanations.art: Three rows of ripple crests drawn at 1, 2 and 4 taps per second with the gaps labelled 30, 15 and 7.5 centimetres.

explanations.concept: Amplitude, energy and why ripples fade
explanations.context: This card is about the height of a wave and the energy it carries.
explanations.definition: The amplitude is how far the wave rises above its flat resting level. A wave with a bigger amplitude carries more energy. As a wave spreads out, the same energy is shared over a longer line, so the wave gets lower.
explanations.description: Drop one marble into a wide basin of still water. A ring of ripples spreads out. The first ring is quite tall. As it grows, it gets wider and lower, until you cannot see it. The energy of the splash is still there, but it is spread over a longer and longer circle, so each bit of the ring has less. Some of the energy also turns into a tiny amount of heat because water rubs against water. Amplitude and frequency are different things. A ripple can be tall and slow, or tiny and fast. How tall it is tells you how much energy it carries. How often it comes is the frequency.
examples: A big wave from a storm carries far more energy than a ripple.
A ring of ripples from a dropped marble gets lower as it grows wider.
A loud sound has a bigger amplitude than a soft sound of the same pitch.
explanations.art: A ring of ripples from a marble with the near ring tall and the far ring low, and arrows showing the energy spreading over a wider circle.

explanations.context: This card names the two kinds of wave you tried with a spring toy and a dupatta, and says where sound and earthquake waves belong.
explanations.definition: In a push wave, the material moves back and forth along the way the wave travels. In a shake wave, the material moves across the way the wave travels. Scientists call these longitudinal and transverse waves.
explanations.description: A spring toy can show both. Squeeze a few coils and let go, and a squeeze runs along. That is a push wave. Flick one end sideways, and a bump runs along. That is a shake wave. Sound in air is a push wave. The air is squeezed together and then spread out as the sound goes by. A shake wave needs a material that holds its shape, like a rope or rock, because the material must be pulled back sideways. Air and water do not hold their shape, so sound in air is only a push wave. Water ripples on top of a pond are a mix of both and make small circles. An earthquake sends both kinds. Scientists call the push kind P waves, because they arrive first. They call the shake kind S waves. P waves can cross liquid, but S waves cannot. That difference was how scientists found that the Earth has a liquid outer core.
examples: Sound in air is a push wave.
A bump along a dupatta is a shake wave.
An earthquake sends P waves, which push, and S waves, which shake. Only the P waves go through the liquid outer core.
explanations.art: A spring toy drawn twice: once with a squeeze running along it, once with a sideways bump, with arrows for the way the wave goes and the way the coils move.

explanations.concept: Light and radio are waves too, and wavelength decides the kind
explanations.context: This card shows that the same rule of speed, frequency and wavelength also fits light and radio.
explanations.definition: Light, radio waves and many other waves are made of changing electric and magnetic effects, and they can cross empty space. All of them travel at the speed of light in empty space, which is about 300,000 kilometres each second. Their wavelength decides what kind they are.
explanations.description: Because every light and radio wave travels at the same speed in empty space, a higher frequency always means a shorter wavelength. Red light is about 700 nanometres long. Violet light is about 400 nanometres long. A hair is about a hundred times wider than a red light wave. Wi-Fi uses waves about 12 centimetres long. An FM radio station at 100 megahertz uses waves about 3 metres long, because 300 million metres each second divided by 100 million is 3 metres. An AM radio station can use waves hundreds of metres long. All of them are the same kind of thing, a rippling of electric and magnetic effects. Only the wavelength differs. Light with a wavelength shorter than violet, which we cannot see, is called ultraviolet. It is what burns skin at the beach.
examples: Red light has a longer wavelength than violet light.
A Wi-Fi box and a microwave oven both use waves about 12 centimetres long.
An FM radio station at 100 megahertz sends waves about 3 metres long.
explanations.art: A long number line of wavelengths from radio towers on the left, through a Wi-Fi box and a rainbow, to a tiny wave on the right, with labels from metres to nanometres.

explanations.concept: Ripples in space itself: gravitational waves
explanations.context: This card goes out to the biggest waves we know, ripples in space and time that scientists first caught in 2015.
explanations.definition: A gravitational wave is a ripple in space and time, made when very heavy things such as black holes move fast. It travels at the speed of light.
explanations.description: In 1916 Albert Einstein's theory of gravity said that heavy things speeding up should send out ripples in space. He thought they would be far too small to find. On 14 September 2015, two giant instruments in the United States, called LIGO, felt a ripple that had been travelling for about 1.3 billion years. It came from two black holes that crashed together. As the ripple passed, the distance between the instruments' mirrors changed by far less than the width of a proton. Scientists announced the find in February 2016. The ripple lasted a fraction of a second, with a frequency that rose from about 35 hertz to about 250 hertz, which is in the range of sounds we can hear. Played as sound, it is a short rising chirp. Indian scientists were part of the team that studied the signal, and India plans a third detector.
examples: Two black holes spiralling together send out ripples in space.
The first ripple caught in 2015 had a frequency that rose from about 35 to about 250 hertz.
Played through a speaker, a gravitational wave signal sounds like a short chirp.
explanations.art: Two black holes spiralling together with rings spreading out in a grid of space, and a pair of long tunnels labelled detector at the edge of the picture.

explanations.concept: A steady beat from the sky: pulsars
explanations.context: This card tells what Jocelyn Bell found in 1967 and what the beat turned out to be.
explanations.definition: A pulsar is a spinning neutron star that sends out beams of radio waves. Each time a beam sweeps across Earth, we receive a pulse. The time between pulses is the star's period.
explanations.description: A neutron star is what is left when a big star runs out of fuel and collapses. It is only about 20 kilometres wide, but it can be heavier than the Sun. Some neutron stars are strongly magnetic, and they send radio beams out of two spots, like a lighthouse. As the star spins, the beams sweep the sky. If a beam sweeps over Earth, a radio telescope hears a pulse once for every spin. The first pulsar found sent a pulse every 1.337 seconds. Others spin much faster. The fastest known spins more than 700 times each second. Pulsars are so steady that astronomers use some of them as clocks. In this way a frequency, a count of beats each second, told people what a distant star was doing.
examples: The first pulsar found sent a pulse about every 1.3 seconds.
The fastest known pulsar spins more than 700 times each second.
Some pulsars keep time so well that astronomers use them as clocks in space.
explanations.art: A pulsar star with two beams sweeping through space and a graph of regular pulses beneath it.

explanations.context: This card shows that living beings keep, use and sense frequencies all the time.
explanations.definition: Many living beings make beats at a steady frequency and use the frequencies of others. Heart rates, wingbeats and calls are all frequencies.
explanations.description: A resting elephant's heart beats about 30 times each minute, while a mouse's heart beats several hundred times each minute. A bee's wings beat roughly 200 times each second, and that makes the buzz you hear. A male mosquito listens for the wingbeat of a female, which is a frequency of about 400 to 500 beats each second, and follows it. Crickets sing faster when the evening is warmer, so you can count their chirps to guess the temperature. Your brain has electrical rhythms too. When you are relaxed with your eyes closed, the main rhythm is around 10 beats each second. A frequency is a way of describing what living beings do, as well as what pendulums do.
examples: A bee's wings beat roughly 200 times each second, which is why she buzzes.
A male mosquito listens for the wingbeat of a female and flies towards it.
A cricket chirps faster on a warm evening and slower on a cool one.
explanations.art: A bee, a mosquito, a cricket and an elephant, each with a small wave line and a number of beats each second.

explanations.concept: Is the beat in the thing, or in the counting?
explanations.context: This card is a question people answer in different ways: is frequency really out in the world?
explanations.description: A pendulum swings once every 2 seconds. Where is the 2 seconds? You can say it is in the pendulum, a fact that was there before anyone counted. Or you can say it is in the counting. Nature has swings and ripples and stars turning, but the second is a unit that people agreed on, and so is the count. A frequency is a swing seen through a human clock. The two views agree on every measurement. They disagree about what the number is.
examples: A pulsar spins at a steady rate whether or not anyone counts it.
The word second, and the number 1.337, come from people agreeing on a clock.

perspectives.explanation: Frequency is a real property of the swinging thing. The pendulum's beat was there before anyone counted it, and the number only says it in a shared language.

perspectives.who: Some philosophers of science, called instrumentalists
perspectives.explanation: Numbers like frequency are tools for predicting what we will see. They are useful, but we should not say nature itself holds them.

explanations.art: A pendulum with a number 2 floating over it, and two children, one pointing at the pendulum and one pointing at the clock.

agreed.text: The frequency of a wave is set by its source, and the speed of a wave is set by the material it travels through.
agreed.evidence: In tray tests with the same tapping rate in different depths, the crests keep the same spacing in time at the source, but travel at the speed of the water. School laboratories use ripple tanks to show this.

agreed.text: Wave speed equals frequency times wavelength.
agreed.evidence: It holds for ripples, sound, radio and light. Measuring any two of the three lets you work out the third, and engineers use it to design radios, loudspeakers and musical instruments.

agreed.text: The time a pendulum takes for one small swing depends on its length and not on its weight or on the width of the swing.
agreed.evidence: Pendulum clocks kept time for centuries on this rule. It was first used in a working clock designed by Christiaan Huygens in the 1650s.

agreed.text: A wave with a bigger amplitude carries more energy.
agreed.evidence: A tall sea wave can knock down a person, and a tiny ripple cannot. Engineers measure wave heights to design harbours and breakwaters.

agreed.text: Light and radio waves are the same kind of wave and differ in wavelength.
agreed.evidence: In 1887 Heinrich Hertz made radio waves in a laboratory and showed they behaved like light, reflecting and bending. Radio and light have both been measured to travel at the same speed in empty space.
The LIGO instruments in the United States caught one on 14 September 2015, and later detectors in Europe and elsewhere have caught many more from crashing black holes and neutron stars.

challenging.claim: A heavier pendulum swings faster, because heavy things fall faster.
challenging.who: A very common first guess, and an old idea taught by the ancient Greek thinker Aristotle about falling things
challenging.for: A heavy stone does feel as if it drops harder and quicker than a feather.
challenging.against: Galileo wrote that a lead ball and a cork ball hung on equal threads swung together. In the Counting Swings test a washer and two washers swing in the same time. A heavier bob is also pulled down harder, but it is harder to move, and the two effects cancel.
challenging.context: This card is about whether the weight of a pendulum changes how fast it swings.

challenging.claim: A faster-moving source makes a faster wave.
challenging.for: A fast thing, like a bowled cricket ball, does go fast because of the way it was thrown.
challenging.against: A finger that taps faster makes more crests each second, but each crest travels at the same speed. The wave speed is set by the water. Only the spacing of the crests changes.
challenging.context: This card is about whether shaking a wave source faster makes the wave itself faster.

challenging.claim: A wave needs something to travel through, so light must travel through an invisible material.
challenging.who: Most physicists in the 1800s, who called the material the ether
challenging.for: Every wave they knew, water, sound and rope, needed a material, so light should too.
challenging.against: In 1887 Albert Michelson and Edward Morley looked for the effect that such a material should have on the speed of light, and found none. Einstein's theory in 1905 worked without it, and light is now understood as a wave of electric and magnetic effects that crosses empty space.
challenging.context: This card is about a wrong idea that light needs an invisible material to travel through.

challenging.claim: The regular beat from the sky was made by a signal from a living civilisation.
challenging.who: A joke in Jocelyn Bell's team in 1967, which they called LGM, for little green men
challenging.for: The signal was far steadier than anything astronomers expected from a star, which seemed like a deliberate clock.
challenging.against: A second beat then appeared in another part of the sky, at a different rate, and then more. It was very unlikely that several unrelated civilisations would send out signals in the same way. Spinning neutron stars explained all of them.
challenging.context: This card is about the first guesses for what made the beat that Jocelyn Bell found.

challenging.claim: Gravitational waves can be used to learn about the objects in the universe that give out no light.
challenging.for: Two black holes give out no light, yet LIGO caught their crash through the ripples they made.
challenging.against: The signals are extremely tiny, and few detectors exist, so scientists cannot yet say exactly where in the sky each signal came from, and they are still working out what they can learn from them.
challenging.context: This card asks whether ripples in space can give us a new way to see the universe.

big_questions.q: A pendulum takes the same time to swing wide as to swing narrow. So who decides how often it swings, you or the pendulum?
big_questions.hint: Think about what you changed in the test and what stayed the same.

big_questions.q: When you tap faster, the ripples get closer together but travel at the same speed. Where did the extra waves go?
big_questions.hint: Count the crests that leave each second, and think about where they are after one second.

big_questions.q: Sound, ripples, radio and light all follow the same rule of speed, frequency and wavelength. Is a wave one thing that shows up in many places, or many different things that follow one rule?
big_questions.hint: Think about what a ripple, a radio wave and a sound are each made of.

big_questions.q: A pulsar spins hundreds of times each second, far away, and we only know it by counting pulses. Can we really know what is out there, if all we get is a count?
big_questions.hint: Think about how Jocelyn Bell decided the beat came from a star and not from Earth.

big_questions.q: Your heart, your breath and your brain each keep their own beat. Do you decide your beats, or do they decide you?
big_questions.hint: Try to change your heartbeat on purpose. Then try to change your breathing.

big_questions.q: A soldier's march across a bridge can make the bridge shake if it matches the bridge's natural beat. Who is responsible when a small thing done at the wrong beat causes a big effect?
big_questions.hint: Think about each person's step, and about the beat of all the steps together.

big_questions.q: We listen to the universe by catching gravitational waves, and we see it by catching light. If we only had radios, how different would the universe look?
big_questions.hint: Each kind of wave gets through different things and shows different things.

big_questions.q: Jocelyn Bell saw the beat first, but the Nobel Prize for the discovery went to her supervisor. Who should get the credit for a discovery?
big_questions.hint: Think about who saw it, who explained it, and who has the power to be heard.

story.title: The Pebble on the Bridge
story.note: A made-up story. The science in it is real. Footbridges do sway, and a crowd that moves in time with the sway can make it grow. In June 2000 the Millennium Bridge in London swayed on its opening days and was closed for about two years to fix it. It is also reported that a bridge near Manchester in England broke in 1831 when soldiers marched across in step, though an inquiry also found a weak iron bolt, and soldiers have been told to break step on bridges ever since.
text: Dechen was nine, and every morning she crossed the Teesta river on the hanging bridge to get to school. The bridge was sixty steps long. It was made of steel cables and wooden planks, and it swayed a little whenever anyone walked on it.

Dechen liked the swaying. She had a game. Tied to the rail near the middle was a long thread with a pebble on the end. Madam Lhamu, her science teacher, had shown her how to make it. When the bridge swayed, the pebble swung.
Dechen counted the swings. She had counted them for a whole year. On a quiet morning the bridge swayed thirty times in a minute, once every two seconds, and it never changed.

"You and your numbers," said her Aunt Pema, who looked after the bridge. Aunt Pema oiled the clamps and tightened the bolts every month. "The bridge is a quiet old lady. She talks in swings, and you are the only one who listens."

One bright morning in the harvest season, a school party came up from the town. There were forty children and their teacher, Mr. Rai, a tall man with a loud voice. They had come to see the bridge, and they were singing a slow song.
It was the kind of song where you rock from one foot to the other. As the children stepped onto the bridge, the whole line began to rock with it, left and right, left and right, laughing.
Dechen was already halfway across, on her way to school. She felt the planks lean. She looked at her pebble. It was swinging much wider than usual.
She began to count. One. Two. The pebble reached the left side at the same moment the children rocked left. One. Two. The children rocked left again, and the bridge leaned further than before.
"It's like a game!" shouted a boy at the back. The planks creaked. A girl stopped laughing. The cables gave a long low groan, and the pebble was swinging so wide that the thread brushed the rail.

Dechen's stomach went tight. She ran back along the bridge, and the planks shook under her feet. "Please stop," she said to the first child she saw. "Please stop singing." But the song was loud, and nobody heard a small girl.

She thought of the swing in the school yard. Madam Lhamu had said, "A swing has its own beat. Push at the right moment, every time, and the swing climbs. Push at the wrong moment, and it goes nowhere."

That was it. The bridge had its own beat, one swing every two seconds. The children were rocking at exactly that beat. Each rock was a tiny push, and every push came just as the bridge was ready for it. So the pushes were adding up.
Dechen ran to Mr. Rai. "Sir," she said, out of breath, "you must make them stop rocking together."
He looked down at her. "The bridge is perfectly safe, little one."

"It is safe when we are all different," said Dechen. "Look." She held up her thread. The pebble was swinging in great sweeps. "The bridge swings once every two seconds. Your children are pushing it every two seconds, all together. If they walk any way they like, the pushes will not match, and the swing will go away."

Mr. Rai looked at the pebble. He looked at the cables, which were humming. He took a deep breath and shouted in his biggest voice, "Stop singing! Everybody walk, but not together! Walk like you are in the market!"
The children laughed, and they walked. Some walked fast and some walked slowly. Some stopped to look at the river. Nobody was in step with anyone.
Dechen watched her pebble. Its swing got smaller. Then it got smaller again. Within a minute it was swinging only a little, just as it did on any quiet morning.
Aunt Pema came hurrying from the far tower, wiping her hands on her skirt. "What was that?" she said. "The whole bridge was dancing."
Dechen showed her the thread. "They were rocking in time with her," she said. "Her beat is one swing every two seconds. Small pushes at the right time add up to a big swing."
Aunt Pema was quiet for a moment. "Years ago, I heard that soldiers must never march in step across a bridge," she said slowly. "I never knew why. Now I think I do."

That evening Dechen counted the swings again, from the very middle of the bridge, with the river roaring below. Thirty in a minute, once every two seconds. The old lady had not changed her beat at all.
story.epiphany: A thing that can swing has a beat of its own. A push that arrives at that beat makes the swing grow, and many small pushes at the right time add up to a big swing. Pushes that arrive at other times do not add up. To stop a swing from growing, you change the beat of the pushes, not the size of the pushes.
ask: How did Dechen find out how often the bridge swayed, and what did she do with that number?
Why did the children's rocking make the bridge sway more, when each child pushed only a little?
Why did the sway fade when the children walked in the market way, though nobody pushed any more gently?
Pushing a child on a swing works the same way as the bridge. When should you push, and why?

roots.context: We have counted swings, tapped ripples and followed the beat out to radio, light and the stars. Now we ask what a beat tells us about the things around us, and about ourselves.

deep_truth.truth: In the swing test, a wide swing and a narrow swing took the same time. How often a pendulum swings comes from the pendulum, not from how hard you push. A push that matches its beat adds up. A push at any other beat does not add up.
deep_truth.habit: We think that pushing harder always makes a thing go faster, and that whoever pushes decides the result. For a swinging thing, the push decides how far it swings, but the thing itself decides how often.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Counting Swings test, ten swings took the same time with a wide swing and a narrow swing, and with one washer and two. Only a longer or shorter string changed the time. If your results differ, write them down as they are and test again.

three.who_am_i: Your heart, your breath and your steps each keep a beat of their own. You can push them a little, but each one also has a rate it likes.
three.what_is_life: A bee, a cricket and a hummingbird each have a wingbeat or a chirp rate that comes from their own bodies. Other living beings listen for those rates, and answer them.
three.what_is_this_world: Ripples, sound, radio and light are all waves, and each has a beat and a length. The same rule of beat, speed and length fits waves in water and waves in space.

roots.thread: A pendulum, a plucked string, a spinning star and a tapping finger all start a wave, and in each one a repeating motion comes first. What the wave travels through then decides how far apart the crests fall. So the spacing in a wave is never made by one thing alone. It comes from a beat meeting a material. The same pattern turns up in a tray of water, in the air of a room, in empty space and in a living body.

teachings.teaching: Heraclitus, an ancient Greek thinker, is reported to have said that different and different waters flow on those who step into the same rivers.
teachings.link: A wave keeps its shape and its beat while the water under it is always new. The pattern stays and the stuff changes.

teachings.teaching: The hymn says that truth is one, and the wise speak of it in many ways.
teachings.link: Ripples, sound, radio and light have different names and different sizes. One rule of beat, speed and length fits them all.

science.text: For every kind of wave measured so far, wave speed equals frequency times wavelength.
Why the universe has so many different kinds of wave, and whether waves are the deepest thing or only a way we describe the deeper thing, is still argued by physicists.

other_view.view: The beat does not belong to the pendulum alone. It comes from the length of the string and the pull of the Earth together. On the Moon, where the pull is weaker, the same pendulum would swing more slowly. So a beat belongs to a thing and its surroundings.

practice.title: Find your own beat
practice.say: Sit still and rest two fingers on the inside of your other wrist, below the thumb. Find the tiny tap of your pulse. Count it for fifteen seconds. Now breathe in slowly and breathe out slowly, and notice whether the taps change. Then sit quietly and listen to your own beat for one more minute.
practice.kid: Find your pulse on your wrist. Count it for fifteen seconds. Breathe slowly in and out. Does the beat change? Listen to it for one minute.

ask: Is the beat of your heart yours, or something your body does for you?
If a pendulum swings differently on the Moon, does it have a beat of its own at all?
Whose beat is a Mexican wave: the first person's, or the crowd's?
roots.art: A child sitting still with two fingers on her wrist, a washer pendulum swinging beside her, and faint rings of ripples and a pulsar beam behind her.

how_we_found_out.story: In 1967 Jocelyn Bell was a research student at Cambridge in England. She helped build a field of wires and posts that listened to radio waves from the sky. It drew long rolls of paper chart every day, and she read them all by eye. One night she spotted a tiny squiggle that she called a bit of scruff. At first the team thought it was interference from something on Earth, such as a car or a radio set. But the squiggle came back each night about four minutes earlier, the way the stars do, so it could not be from Earth. When she ran the chart faster, she saw a string of pulses about 1.3 seconds apart, as steady as a clock. Many astronomers thought no star could beat so evenly. The team joked that it might be little green men. Then Bell found a second beat in another part of the sky, and then more. Scientists soon agreed they were spinning neutron stars. The Nobel Prize in 1974 went to her supervisor, Antony Hewish, who shared it with Martin Ryle, and not to her.
how_we_found_out.who: Jocelyn Bell Burnell (born 1943), an astronomer from Northern Ireland
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Many thought the regular beat must be interference from Earth, or that no natural star could beat so steadily. She showed it followed star time, and the second beat showed it came from a new kind of star.

games.title: Faster or Slower? How often does it repeat?
games.context: This is a card game about frequency. Each card shows something that repeats, and you guess whether it repeats faster or slower than the card before.

setup.art: Twenty-four cards and eight tokens spread on a table, with a pile of cards face down and two cards laid side by side face up.
setup.caption: 1. Cut out the 24 cards and 8 tokens. Shuffle the cards into a pile.

setup.art: A child reading the front of a card aloud, while a parent holds up a Faster token and a Slower token.
setup.caption: 2. Read the new card. Everyone chooses Faster or Slower.

setup.art: A long row of cards laid out in a line from slowest on the left to fastest on the right, with a clock at one end and a star at the other.
setup.caption: 3. At the end, lay all the cards in a line from slowest to fastest.

printables.title: 24 two-sided cards: something that repeats on the front, and about how often on the back

items.f: The Earth turning once all the way round
items.b: About once each day. That is far slower than the tick of a clock, which is once each second.

items.f: The Moon going once round the Earth
items.b: About once each month. A very, very slow beat.

items.f: A sea wave arriving at the beach
items.b: About once every 8 seconds. Sea waves often arrive every 6 to 12 seconds.

items.f: A child on a playground swing
items.b: About one swing every 3 to 4 seconds, because the chains are long.

items.f: A pendulum 1 metre long
items.b: One swing every 2 seconds, which is half a hertz.

items.f: A person blinking
items.b: About 15 times each minute, so about once every 4 seconds.

items.f: A wall clock ticking
items.b: Once each second. That is 1 hertz.

items.f: The heart of a resting child
items.b: About 80 to 100 beats each minute, which is about one and a half beats each second.

items.f: A person walking briskly
items.b: About 2 steps each second.

items.f: A crow flapping her wings in flight
items.b: About 3 or 4 flaps each second.

items.f: A ceiling fan at full speed
items.b: Roughly 5 or 6 turns each second.

items.f: A small hummingbird's wings
items.b: Around 80 beats each second. Bigger hummingbirds are slower, about 20 to 50.

items.f: The mains electricity in an Indian home
items.b: 50 back-and-forth cycles each second. That is 50 hertz.

items.f: A bee's wings
items.b: Roughly 200 beats each second. That is the buzz you hear.

items.f: The wings of a female mosquito
items.b: About 500 beats each second (some kinds 400 to 600). That is the whine you hear.

items.f: The A string on a violin, tuned to concert pitch
items.b: 440 shakes each second.

items.f: Middle C on a piano
items.b: About 262 shakes each second.

items.f: A bat's squeak while hunting
items.b: Often 20,000 to 100,000 each second, too high for people to hear.

items.f: A police whistle
items.b: About 3,000 shakes each second.

items.f: The fastest known spinning star, a pulsar
items.b: More than 700 spins each second.

items.f: The radio waves of an FM station at 100 megahertz
items.b: 100 million each second.

items.f: A mobile phone signal
items.b: Around 1 to 2 billion each second.

items.f: A Wi-Fi box
items.b: About 2.4 billion waves each second.

items.f: The green light from a leaf
items.b: About 500 trillion waves each second.

printables.title: 8 tokens: four that say Faster and four that say Slower

rules: Shuffle the cards and put them in a pile with the front side up. Each player takes one Faster token and one Slower token. Two players need two of each.
The first player turns the top card over and reads both sides aloud. This is the anchor card, and everyone can see how often it repeats.
The next player reads the front of the new top card out loud, but does not turn it over.
Every player puts one token face down. Faster means the new card repeats more often than the anchor. Slower means it repeats less often.
Everyone turns their tokens over together. The reader turns the new card over and reads the back. Players who were right keep one point.
The new card becomes the anchor. Play on until the pile is gone.
At the end, lay all the cards in a line from slowest to fastest. Check the order together, and find the two cards with the biggest jump between them.
Playing alone, hold the anchor in your hand and guess for every card. Try to get 20 out of 23 right.

flow.do: Cut out the cards and the tokens. Shuffle the cards and put them front side up. Give each player one Faster token and one Slower token.
flow.say: In this game, every card shows something that repeats. We will guess whether each new card repeats faster or slower than the one before. Cut out the cards and the tokens first.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards and tokens. Shuffle the cards. Take one Faster and one Slower.
flow.context: This is the first step of Faster or Slower. You get the cards and tokens ready.
flow.parent: No printer? Write each front and back on a paper slip (about 15 minutes, a good job for older children). For 2 to 4 players, each player takes one Faster and one Slower token; with more than 4 players, share in pairs. The numbers on the cards are typical values, not exact.

flow.do: Turn over a clock card. Read both sides as the anchor. Then read the front of the heart card, and let your child choose a token.
flow.say: The clock card ticks once each second. The next card is the heart of a resting child. Does it beat faster or slower than the clock ticks? Choose a token and turn it over.
flow.kid: A clock ticks once a second. A child's heart beats about one and a half. Faster or slower?

check.q: A clock ticks once each second. A resting child's heart beats about 90 times each minute. Which repeats more often?
check.why: 90 beats a minute is one and a half beats each second, which is more than one tick each second. To compare, put both in the same time, such as each second. If you picked the clock, you may have compared 1 with 90 and forgotten that one is each second and one is each minute.

flow.context: In this step, you play one practice round so you know how scoring works.

flow.do: Play the rest of the pile. After every four cards, ask the question below. Keep a score of right guesses.
flow.say: Read the front, choose a token, then turn it over together. Who was right? Then the new card becomes the anchor.
flow.kid: Read the front. Pick a token. Turn it over. Check the back.

ask.q: Which card surprised you most, and why?
good: The hummingbird, because I did not know wings could beat that fast.
The Earth turning, because I forgot it is only once a day.
The mosquito, because the whine is made by wings.

flow.parent: Children often guess a living thing is faster than a machine. Let them be surprised. Do not explain in the middle of the game.
flow.context: In this step, you play through the whole pile and score your guesses.

flow.do: Lay all the cards in a line from the slowest to the fastest. Check your line using the back of each card.
flow.say: Now lay all the cards in a line from slowest to fastest. Where do you think the biggest jump is? Check the backs.
flow.kid: Line up all the cards from slowest to fastest. Find the biggest jump.

check.q: In the line, the ceiling fan, the bee, the violin string and the police whistle are all in a row. Which one repeats most often?
check.why: A fan turns about 5 or 6 times each second, a bee beats her wings about 200 times, and a police whistle shakes about 3,000 times. The more shakes each second, the higher the pitch you hear. A student who picks the fan may be thinking of the largest and slowest thing, which is the fan.

flow.context: In this step, you put all the cards in order from slowest to fastest.

flow.do: Look at the line together. Ask the question below, and let your child answer before you say anything.
flow.say: Look at the line. Some things beat once a day. Some things beat billions of times a second. What do you notice about the cards at the fast end?
flow.kid: Look at the fast end of the line. What kinds of things are there?

ask.q: What kinds of things are at the fast end of the line?
good: Waves, like radio and light.
Things you can hear, like whistles and wings.
Things too small or too fast to see.

flow.parent: The slow end is full of big things, such as the Earth and the Moon. The fast end is full of waves. Light and radio repeat so fast that we cannot count them, but we know it from their wavelength.

experiments.title: Counting Swings: what decides how often a pendulum swings?
experiments.context: In this experiment you hang a washer on a thread and time 10 swings, changing one thing at a time, to find out what decides how often a pendulum swings.
experiments.question: Three things could change how long a pendulum takes to swing: the length of the thread, the weight on the end, and how wide you swing it. Which of the three really does?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. For each of the three, will it make the pendulum take more time, less time, or the same time? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Change only one thing at a time. Always let go of the washer without pushing it. Always time 10 swings, from the moment you let go. Measure the length from the knot at the top to the middle of the washer. Do every test twice, because a stopwatch can start a little late. The washer is the same washer unless the test is about weight.
results_table: My guess: more, same or less time?

materials.item: a strong cotton thread or thin string, about 1.5 metres long
3 steel washers or nuts about 2 centimetres wide (a hardware shop sells them for a few rupees), or 3 one- or two-rupee coins with the thread taped on
cello tape or masking tape, a roll
a door frame, a window grill bar or a high shelf edge to hang the thread from
a measuring tape or a metre ruler
a phone with a stopwatch (a separate stopwatch is not needed)
a pencil and paper for the results table

experiments.safety: A grown-up fixes the thread high up. Everyone stands to the side of the swing, never in front of it, because a steel washer that hits a face can hurt. Switch the ceiling fan off, because moving air spoils the swing.

schedule.what: Time 10 swings for three lengths. Then change the weight, and then the width, and compare.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then finish these sentences: 'The longer the thread, the ...' and 'Changing the weight or the width made ...'

flow.do: Show your child the washer, the thread and the stopwatch. Ask for a guess and a reason for each of the three things. Write the guesses in the table.
flow.say: We will hang a washer on a thread. Three things might change how long it takes to swing: a longer thread, a heavier washer, or a wider swing. For each one, will the swing take more time, less time or the same? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: A washer on a thread. Will a longer thread, a heavier washer or a wider swing change the time? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think a wider swing will take longer?
good: It has further to go.
It goes faster, so it takes the same time.
It is the same washer, so the same.

flow.parent: Do not correct any guess. Many children say a heavier washer swings faster, and many say a wider swing takes longer. Write each guess with its reason so you can come back to it.
flow.context: This is the first step of Counting Swings. You guess before you test.

flow.do: Tape the top of the thread to the top of a door frame. Tie a washer to the other end. Measure from the tape to the middle of the washer. Adjust the knot until it is exactly 100 centimetres.
flow.say: A grown-up fixes the thread to the top of the door frame. The washer hangs free and still. Measure from the top to the middle of the washer. It must be 100 centimetres.
flow.kid: Tape the thread high up. Tie on the washer. Measure to the middle of the washer.
flow.parent: A door frame is about 2 metres high, so a 100 centimetre pendulum has plenty of room. If you have no door frame, hang the thread from a window grill bar or from a broom laid between two chairs. Check that the washer swings without touching anything.

check.q: Why do we measure the length to the middle of the washer, and not to the top of it?
options: The washer's weight acts at its middle
The top is harder to measure
It does not matter where we measure
check.why: The whole washer swings, and it behaves as if its weight were at its middle. If you measured to the top one time and to the middle another time, the lengths would differ by a centimetre, and the timings would be a little off.

flow.context: In this step, you hang the first pendulum and set its length.

flow.do: Pull the washer about 10 centimetres to one side and let go. Do not push. Start the stopwatch as you let go. Count 10 swings and stop. Write the time. Do it twice. Then repeat with threads of 50 centimetres and 25 centimetres.
flow.say: Pull the washer back a little and let go. Do not push it. Start the stopwatch at the moment you let go. One swing is out and all the way back. Count to ten, then stop.
flow.kid: Pull back the washer. Let go. Count 10 swings. Stop the stopwatch. Write the time.
flow.parent: The expected times for 10 swings are about 20 seconds for 100 centimetres, about 14 seconds for 50 centimetres and about 10 seconds for 25 centimetres. A little difference is fine. If the swing wobbles in a circle, start again, and let go from a still hand. Shorten the thread by tying a knot, or tape the thread higher or lower, and always measure again. With two or more children, share the jobs: one lets go, one watches the stopwatch and calls start and stop, one counts the swings aloud, and one writes. Swap jobs for every new length. If you are alone with a parent, the parent counts aloud and the child holds the stopwatch. Use a thread that does not stretch, and tape it firmly so the top does not slip. These times are typical; yours may differ by a second.

check.q: A pendulum takes 20 seconds for 10 swings. How long does one swing take?
check.why: 20 seconds divided by 10 swings is 2 seconds for each swing. We time 10 swings instead of one, because a stopwatch started a quarter of a second late matters much less over 20 seconds than over 2.

flow.context: In this step, you time 10 swings for three different lengths of thread.

flow.do: Go back to the 50 centimetre thread. Tape a second washer to the first so they hang as one. Time 10 swings twice. Compare with the one-washer time.
flow.say: Same thread, same swing. Now the washer is twice as heavy. Time 10 swings. Is it faster, slower or the same?
flow.kid: Tape on a second washer. Time 10 swings. Is it faster, slower or the same?
flow.parent: The time stays about the same, within half a second. Heavier does not mean faster. If the time is quite different, check that the tape is not changing the length of the pendulum. If you have all three washers, tape on both extra ones so the weight is three times as much; the time should still stay about the same.
flow.context: In this step, you change only the weight, to see if the beat changes.

flow.do: Take off the extra washer. With the 50 centimetre thread, pull the washer 5 centimetres to the side and time 10 swings. Then pull it 25 centimetres to the side and time 10 swings. Do each twice.
flow.say: Now a small swing and a big swing. Time 10 swings of each. Which takes longer? Watch the stopwatch carefully.
flow.kid: Time 10 small swings. Then time 10 big swings. Which takes longer?
flow.parent: The two times will be within about half a second of each other. The big swing travels further but moves faster, so it takes about the same time. Keep the big swing to no more than 25 centimetres to the side. For very wide swings the time does grow a little.
flow.context: In this step, you change only how wide the swing is.

flow.do: Look at the table together. Ask your child to say three things: what I think now, what I saw, and why.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What do you think now? What numbers show it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say three things. What I think now. What I saw. Why.

check.q: In your test, which one thing changed how long 10 swings took?
check.why: Longer thread gave a longer time for 10 swings. A second washer gave about the same time, and a wide swing gave about the same time as a small one. Many people expect weight or width to matter. A heavier washer is pulled down harder, but it is also harder to move, and the two cancel.

flow.parent: A strong answer sounds like this: 'The length of the thread changed the time. 25 centimetres took about 10 seconds for 10 swings, and 100 centimetres took about 20. Weight and width did not change it. I think the pendulum has its own beat that comes from its length.' Now read the card 'What sets the beat of a pendulum'.
flow.context: In this step, you say what you found, with evidence and a reason.

experiments.title: Tap Faster: what happens to the ripples?
experiments.context: In this experiment you tap a tray of shallow water at different speeds, and look at how far apart the ripples are.
experiments.question: If you tap the water faster, what happens to the distance between one ripple and the next?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. When you tap faster, will the ripples be closer together, further apart, or the same distance apart? Will they travel faster? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use the same tray, the same ruler edge and the same depth of water, 1 centimetre, every time. Dip the ruler edge into the water the same small distance, about 3 millimetres, on every click. Only the tap rate changes. Measure the gap between ripples three times for each rate, because ripples are hard to see and a single measurement can be wrong. Check the depth at all four corners: if the tray is tilted the depth changes from one end to the other, and the ripples change with it.
results_table: My guess: ripples closer, further, or same?

materials.item: a long tray or plastic box at least 35 centimetres long and with a flat bottom, such as a rectangular baking tray, a big steel parat or vadam-drying tray, or a plastic storage box, with a light-coloured or clear bottom (buy one only if you have nothing like it)
water, enough for about 1 centimetre depth
a 30 centimetre ruler to dip in the water, and another ruler or tape to measure the gaps
a phone with a free metronome app, set to 120, 180 and 240 beats a minute (any free metronome website on a computer also works)
a torch (a phone torch is fine), propped on a stack of books about 40 to 50 centimetres above the tray, and a dimly lit room
a sheet of white paper to put under a clear tray
a folded old towel or a sponge to soak up waves at the far end
an old towel to stand the tray on
a second phone or a camera, to photograph the ripples from above (the grown-up's phone is fine)
a jug or mug to pour the water

experiments.safety: Wipe up any spilt water at once, because a wet floor is slippery. Keep a small child away from the tray and do not use it near plug sockets. Switch the fan off, because moving air spoils the ripples.

schedule.what: Tap the same tray at 2, 3 and 4 taps each second. Measure the gap between the ripples each time, and compare.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Circle the middle gap for each rate. Then finish this sentence: 'The faster I tapped, the ...'

flow.do: Show your child the tray, the ruler and the metronome. Ask for a guess and a reason. Write the guess at the top of the table.
flow.say: We will dip a ruler into a tray of water again and again, to a beat. Then we will tap faster. Will the ripples be closer together, further apart, or the same? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Tap faster. Will the ripples be closer, further apart, or the same? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think the ripples will be that way?
good: Faster taps push the ripples closer together.
Faster taps make the ripples go faster, so they spread out.
The water is the same, so the ripples stay the same.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Children often say faster taps make the ripples travel faster and so spread out. Write the guess and the reason. You will come back to it.
flow.context: This is the first step of Tap Faster. You guess before you test.

flow.do: Put the tray on a towel on a flat floor. Pour in water until it is 1 centimetre deep. Check the depth at both ends with a ruler. Lay a folded towel at the far end. Put white paper under a clear tray. Dim the room.
flow.say: Pour in water until it is exactly 1 centimetre deep at both ends. Then lay the folded towel at the far end. It soaks up the ripples, so they do not bounce back.
flow.kid: Pour 1 centimetre of water. Lay a towel at the far end. Make the room dim.
flow.parent: The floor must be flat, or the water will be deeper at one end. If your tray is dark steel, the ripples will show as moving reflections of the torch on the ceiling and wall. Shine the torch from the side across the water and look at the bright lines on the tray bottom or the wall. A 35 by 25 centimetre tray needs about 1 litre of water for 1 centimetre. A tray on a hard flat table is steadier than one on a soft towel, so use the towel only to catch spills. A dished or bent bottom spoils the result; choose the flattest tray. Switch the fan off.
flow.context: In this step, you get the tray ready.

flow.do: Switch on the metronome at 120 beats a minute. Hold the ruler flat across the near end of the tray, with one long edge just touching the water. On each click, press the edge 3 millimetres into the water. Lift it out with a small flick of the wrist. Hold the torch 40 to 50 centimetres above the tray. Bright and dark lines show on the paper under it, or on the wall.
flow.say: The metronome clicks twice each second. On every click, dip the edge of the ruler into the water and lift it out. Shine the torch and look for bright lines moving away from the ruler.
flow.kid: Dip the ruler on every click. Shine the torch. Look for lines moving away.
flow.parent: Each dip sends a straight ripple down the tray. The bright lines are the crests. Take your time: it takes a minute to get a steady rhythm. If you cannot see lines, tilt the torch lower, dim the room more, or look at the lines on the wall. If ripples bounce back from the far end, make the towel thicker. Roles for 2 to 4 children: one taps, one keeps the metronome and checks the depth, one holds the torch and takes the photos, one measures and writes. Alone with a parent, the child taps and the parent photographs. If you see nothing: make the room darker, move the torch lower and further away, tap a little harder, and make sure the water is still before you start. If the tray is dark steel, the lines will not show on the bottom; look at the moving bright lines on the wall instead. If you still cannot see lines, your ripples are probably too faint: use a bigger dip and keep the water 1 centimetre deep.

check.q: At 120 clicks a minute, how many dips do you make each second?
check.why: 120 clicks in 60 seconds is 2 clicks each second. If you picked 120, you forgot to divide by the 60 seconds in a minute.

flow.context: In this step, you make your first set of ripples, at 2 taps each second.

flow.do: Take a photo (or a short video) from straight above with a ruler lying on the paper under the tray along the way the ripples travel. Find three bright lines in a row in the photo and measure from the first to the third. Divide by 2 for the gap. Do this three times. If the tray is too short for three lines, measure from the first to the second line. Then set the metronome to 180 and 240 beats a minute, and repeat.
flow.say: Three bright lines in a row have two gaps. Measure from the first to the third, and halve it. Do it three times. Then speed the metronome up and do it again.
flow.kid: Take a photo from above. Measure from the first line to the third. Halve it. Do it three times. Then tap faster.
flow.parent: Expect gaps of about 12 to 16 centimetres at 2 taps each second, about 9 or 10 at 3, and about 6 to 8 at 4. Your numbers may differ with your tray, but the gaps must shrink as the taps speed up. A phone photo from above, with the ruler laid beside the tray, helps you measure after the ripples have gone. At 4 taps each second, tap lightly with a small dip so the ripples stay clean. Measuring from a photo is far easier than trying to measure moving ripples by eye. At 4 taps each second the dips are quick; practise a little flick and tap lightly. These gaps are typical; your tray may give gaps a few centimetres different, but they must shrink as the taps get faster.
flow.context: In this step, you measure the gap between ripples at three different tap rates.

flow.do: Look at the table together. Ask your child to say three things: what I think now, what I saw, and why.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What do you think now? What numbers show it? And why do you think it happened? Remember that in the tray the water set the speed, and you set how often.
flow.kid: Say three things. What I think now. What I saw. Why.

check.q: At 4 taps each second, the gaps were about half the gaps at 2 taps each second. What stayed the same?
options: How fast the ripples travelled across the water
How many ripples were made each second
check.why: The water was the same depth, so the ripples travelled at the same speed. Twice as many ripples were made each second, so they had to fit into the same distance, and each one was half as far from the next. Picking 'how many ripples' is a natural slip, because it is the thing that you changed.

flow.parent: A strong answer sounds like this: 'The faster I tapped, the closer the ripples got. At 2 taps they were about 14 centimetres apart, and at 4 taps about 7. I think the water makes the ripples go at one speed, and my taps decide how many fit in each stretch.' Now read the card 'Wavelength comes from speed and frequency'.
flow.context: In this step, you say what you found, with evidence and a reason.

activities.title: Hertz Hunt: how often does it happen?
activities.context: This is a short activity to start the unit. You count how often a few things repeat, and turn each count into a number each second.

materials.item: a phone with a stopwatch, or a clock with a seconds hand
a pencil and a sheet of paper for a table
a chair to sit on while you count

schedule.what: Count your pulse, your breaths and your steps. Turn each count into a number of times each second.

activities.record: A table with three rows: pulse, breaths and steps. For each, write the count, the time, and the number each second.

flow.do: Show your child how to find a pulse on the wrist, below the thumb. Ask them to guess how many beats there are in 15 seconds. Write the guess down.
flow.say: Your heart beats all day. Put two fingers on your wrist, below the thumb, until you feel a tiny tap. How many taps do you think you will feel in 15 seconds? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Find your pulse. Guess how many taps in 15 seconds. Why?

ask.q: Why do you think it will be that many?
good: My heart feels fast, so maybe 20.
I do not know, I will guess about 10.
A clock ticks once a second, so maybe 15.

flow.parent: Do not worry about the guess. A resting child's pulse is usually about 18 to 25 beats in 15 seconds. If your child cannot find it, try the other wrist, or help them find it. Press lightly with two fingers, never hard, and never on the neck.
flow.context: This is the first step of Hertz Hunt. You guess, and then you count your pulse.

flow.do: Sit still for one minute. Then count the pulse taps for 15 seconds. Write down the count. Multiply by 4 for beats each minute. Divide by 60 for beats each second.
flow.say: Sit still and be calm. Count the taps for 15 seconds, and I will tell you when to stop. Then we multiply by 4 to get one minute.
flow.kid: Sit still. Count your pulse for 15 seconds. Multiply by 4.
flow.parent: A count of 22 in 15 seconds gives 88 beats each minute. 88 divided by 60 is about 1.5 beats each second, a frequency of about 1.5 hertz. Dividing is hard for some children. Use a calculator, or say: 60 beats is one each second, so 88 is a little more than one each second. With 2 to 4 children, work in pairs: one counts a pulse while the other times 15 seconds, then swap. Compare everyone's answers: pulse rates differ and that is normal.

check.q: A pulse count is 20 beats in 15 seconds. How many beats is that in one minute?
check.why: One minute is four lots of 15 seconds, so 20 times 4 is 80 beats. If you picked 35 you added 15 instead of multiplying by 4.

flow.context: In this step, you count your pulse and work out beats each minute.

flow.do: Count your breaths for 30 seconds. One breath is in and out. Multiply by 2 for breaths each minute. Then walk on the spot for 10 seconds and count your steps.
flow.say: Breathe normally. Count each breath, in and out, for 30 seconds. Then we will march on the spot for 10 seconds and count the steps.
flow.kid: Count your breaths for 30 seconds. Then march for 10 seconds and count steps.
flow.parent: Children usually breathe 8 to 12 times in 30 seconds, which is 16 to 24 breaths each minute, around one third of a hertz. Steady marching is about 2 steps each second, so about 20 steps in 10 seconds. Do not tell your child these numbers before they count.
flow.context: In this step, you count your breaths and your steps.

flow.do: Fill in the table together. For each row, write how many times each second. Put the rows in order from the slowest to the fastest.
flow.say: Look at your table. Which of your three things repeats most often each second, and which least often? Why do you think that is?
flow.kid: Which repeats most often? Which least often? Put them in order.
flow.think: Which of your three beats can you change on purpose, and which can you hardly change at all?
flow.parent: Expect order: breath (about 0.3 hertz), pulse (about 1.5 hertz), steps (about 2 hertz). A pulse can be changed a little by running. Breath is the beat we can change most easily. This is the idea of frequency, and you will meet it again with pendulums and ripples.

activities.title: The Wave Grid: shift and colour
activities.context: In this paper activity you colour a grid to model a wave moving along a line. You find out how the beat and the speed decide the wavelength.

materials.item: squared paper, such as a page of a squared maths notebook, or plain paper and a ruler to draw grids of squares about 1 centimetre wide
a pencil or crayon to colour with
a coloured pen to mark the gaps
a ruler

schedule.what: Colour three grids. Change the beat in the second and the speed in the third. Measure the gap between coloured squares in each.

activities.record: Three coloured grids. Under each, write the beat, the speed and the gap between coloured squares in a row.

flow.do: Draw a grid with 12 columns and 12 rows. Number the rows 1 to 12 down the side. Each row is one beat of time. The columns are places along a line.
flow.say: This grid shows a line of 12 places. Each row down is one beat of time. A wave-maker stands at the left end, and we will see what the wave does as the beats go by.
flow.kid: Draw a grid. 12 columns across. 12 rows down. Number the rows.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Wave Grid. You make the grid.

flow.do: In row 1, colour the left square. In each row below, copy the row above, but slide every colour one square to the right. Colour the left square again in rows 5 and 9 only.
flow.say: The rule is simple. Copy the row above and slide every coloured square one place to the right. The wave-maker adds a new coloured square at the left end every fourth row.
flow.kid: Copy each row, sliding colours one right. Add a new left square every 4th row.
flow.parent: You should see slanting stripes. In every row the coloured squares are 4 apart. That is the wavelength: 4 squares. The wave moves at 1 square each beat, and the source makes a new crest every 4 beats, so one wave stretches over 4 squares.

check.q: In your grid, the wave moves 1 square each beat, and the wave-maker colours a new square every 4 beats. How far apart are the coloured squares in a row?
check.why: In 4 beats, the first coloured square slides 4 places before the next one begins. So the coloured squares are 4 apart. If you chose 1, you used the wave speed and forgot the beat of the wave-maker.

flow.context: In this step, you colour the first grid, with a new crest every 4 beats.

flow.do: Draw a second grid with the same slide rule. This time, colour the left square every second row. Measure the gap between coloured squares in one row.
flow.say: The wave-maker now beats twice as often, every second row. Before you colour, guess. Will the coloured squares be closer together or further apart? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: New beat: colour the left square every 2nd row. Guess the gap first.
flow.parent: The coloured squares are now 2 squares apart. A faster beat with the same speed gives a shorter wavelength. This matches the ripples in your tray.
flow.context: In this step, you make the wave-maker beat twice as fast, and see what happens to the gap.

flow.do: Draw a third grid, 16 squares wide and 12 rows down. Slide each row two squares to the right instead of one. Colour the left square in rows 1, 5 and 9, as in the first grid. Measure the gap between coloured squares in the lower rows.
flow.say: Now the wave moves faster, two places each beat. The wave-maker beats every 4 rows, as before. Guess the gap before you colour. Closer, further, or the same?
flow.kid: Slide two squares each row. Colour the left every 4th row. Guess the gap.
flow.parent: The coloured squares are now 8 apart. A faster wave with the same beat gives a longer wavelength. The gap is the speed (2 squares each beat) times the 4 beats between crests. This is the rule: wavelength is speed times the time between beats. The third grid needs 16 columns so that two crests are on the page together. With 2 to 4 children, each draws one grid and the group compares; alone with a parent, take turns colouring a row each.

check.q: A wave moves 2 squares each beat, and the source makes a crest every 3 beats. How far apart will the crests be?
check.why: In 3 beats the first crest moves 2 squares each beat, which is 2 times 3, or 6 squares, before the next crest begins. So the crests are 6 apart. Adding the numbers to get 5 is a common slip.

flow.context: In this step, you make the wave twice as fast, and see how the gap changes.
