activities.title: Rainbow from a CD: light has wavelengths too
activities.context: In this activity you spread white light into a rainbow, and see that different colours are different wavelengths.

materials.item: an old CD or DVD that you no longer need (a blank CD costs a few rupees at a computer or stationery shop)
a torch or a phone torch in a dim room, or bright sunshine through a window
a white wall or a sheet of white paper
optional: a tall clear glass of water (a bonus that works only in strong sun)

activities.safety: Never look straight at the Sun, and never shine sunlight or a torch into anyone's eyes. Keep the shiny side of the CD pointing at the wall, not at faces. Use a CD with no cracks, because a broken edge is sharp. Use a plastic cup or a strong glass for the water, and a grown-up stays close. Do not leave a glass of water in strong sun near paper or cloth, because it can focus the sunlight into a hot spot.

schedule.what: Shine light on the shiny side of a CD to make a rainbow on a wall. Name the colours in order. Match each colour to a wavelength.

activities.record: Draw the rainbow in order. Write 'longest waves' under the red end and 'shortest waves' under the violet end.

flow.do: Hold the CD with its shiny side, the side without a label, facing the light. Tilt it until a band of colours shows on the wall. Ask your child what they see.
flow.say: Here is an old CD. Let the light fall on the shiny side and tilt it slowly. What do you see on the wall? Which colour is at which end?
flow.kid: Tilt the CD in the light. Look at the wall. What colours do you see?

ask.q: Which colour is at each end of the rainbow?
good: Red at one end and violet at the other.
Red on the outside and blue or violet on the inside.

flow.parent: The CD has tiny grooves that spread white light into its colours. In a dim room, a phone torch about 20 centimetres from the CD gives a sharp rainbow on a wall 1 metre away. If you cannot make it work, try holding the CD at different angles. In bright sunshine, the effect is strongest. It works best with the room darkened, the torch about 20 centimetres from the CD, and the wall about 1 metre away. With 2 to 4 children: one holds the CD, one holds the torch, one marks the band on the wall with a pencil or a sticky note, one draws it. If you see only a white blur, tilt the CD slowly; the colours show only at one angle.
flow.context: This is the first step of the CD Rainbow. You make a rainbow and look at its colours.

flow.do: Write down the colours in order along the band, starting from the end nearest the bright spot of reflected light. Measure the width of the band on the wall. Then move back so the CD is twice as far from the wall, and measure the band again. If it is sunny, you can also try the glass of water.
flow.say: Say the colours in order: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, violet. Red has the longest waves, about 700 nanometres. Violet has the shortest, about 400 nanometres.
flow.kid: Say the colours in order. Red has the longest waves. Violet has the shortest.
flow.parent: A nanometre is a billionth of a metre. A hair is about a hundred times wider than a red light wave. The glass of water works best when a beam of sunshine passes through it onto a white paper. Move the glass until a rainbow appears. On a CD, red is the end furthest from the bright spot, because longer waves spread out more; a prism or a raindrop does the opposite. The band should be about twice as wide when the wall is twice as far away, because light travels in straight lines. The glass of water often fails: it needs strong, low sunshine and some luck, so do not worry if nothing appears.

check.q: Which colour of visible light has the longest wavelength?
check.why: Red light has a wavelength of about 700 nanometres, the longest we can see. Violet is about 400 nanometres, the shortest. If you chose violet, you may be thinking that violet is more energetic, which is true, but its waves are shorter.

flow.context: In this step, you name the colours in order and match them to wavelengths.

flow.do: Ask your child to think about what stays the same for all the colours, and what is different. Let them answer before you give any answer.
flow.say: All these colours travel at the same speed in empty space. Red and violet differ in how long their waves are. What does that tell you about how often their waves come each second?
flow.kid: Red and violet travel at the same speed. Which has more waves each second?
flow.think: If all the colours travel at the same speed, which colour must have the most waves each second?
flow.parent: Violet. Shorter waves at the same speed means more waves arrive each second. Violet light has a frequency around 750 trillion each second, and red around 430 trillion. These numbers are too large to picture, so just notice that violet is higher.

activities.title: The Wavelength Ladder: from ripples to light
activities.context: In this activity you sort ten kinds of wave by wavelength, from the longest to the shortest, and see the full family of waves.

materials.item: 10 small slips of paper or card
a pen
a long strip of paper or a hallway floor to lay the slips on
a calculator, or pencil and paper for the sums

schedule.what: Guess the order of ten waves by wavelength. Check with the numbers. Work out two wavelengths yourself with the speed rule.

activities.record: A ladder of ten slips in order, with a rough wavelength written on each. Circle the two that surprised you.

flow.do: Write each wave on its own slip. The ten waves are a sea wave, a ripple in a tray, a human voice, a police whistle and FM radio. The rest are AM radio, Wi-Fi, a microwave oven, red light and a tsunami.
flow.say: Each slip names a kind of wave. Put them in a line, from the longest wavelength to the shortest. It is only a guess for now. Why do you put each one where you do?
flow.kid: Put the ten slips in a line. Longest on the left. Shortest on the right.

ask.q: Which wave do you think has the longest wavelength, and why?
good: The tsunami, because it is the biggest wave.
The radio, because it travels a long way.
The sea wave, because it is so big.

flow.parent: Do not correct the order. Children often put light near the longest end. Write down the order before checking. Here is the real order, longest first, with rough lengths: tsunami over 100 kilometres, AM radio about 300 metres, sea wave about 100 metres, FM radio about 3 metres, human voice about 1.7 metres, Wi-Fi and microwave oven about 12 centimetres, police whistle about 11 centimetres, ripple in a tray about 10 centimetres, red light about 0.0000007 metres. All of these lengths are rough, typical values. With 2 to 4 children, each child lays out their own ladder first, then the group compares and argues before checking. Alone, the child lays it out and the parent asks 'why there?'.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Wavelength Ladder. You guess the order of ten waves.

flow.do: Check your order using the numbers in the parent note. Move any slip that is in the wrong place. Write the rough wavelength on each slip. Circle the two that surprised you.
flow.say: Now we check. Write the rough wavelength on each slip, and move any that were wrong. Which two surprised you most?
flow.kid: Check the order. Fix any wrong slip. Circle two surprises.
flow.parent: Surprises to expect: a Wi-Fi box, a microwave oven and a police whistle are all within a few centimetres of each other, although they are very different waves. A tsunami's wavelength is over 100 kilometres, longer than many cities are wide. Light is a hundred times thinner than a hair.

check.q: Which of these has the shortest wavelength?
check.why: Red light is about 0.0000007 metres, much shorter than the whistle at about 11 centimetres, or the FM radio wave at about 3 metres. Light is the smallest because its frequency is so high: hundreds of trillions of waves each second.

flow.context: In this step, you check your order against real numbers.

flow.do: Work out two wavelengths yourself. Sound travels about 340 metres each second in air. A voice at 200 hertz: divide 340 by 200. A whistle at 3,000 hertz: divide 340 by 3,000.
flow.say: Use the rule: wavelength is speed divided by frequency. A voice at 200 hertz has a wavelength of 340 divided by 200. A whistle at 3,000 hertz is 340 divided by 3,000. Use a calculator if you like.
flow.kid: Divide 340 by 200 for the voice. Divide 340 by 3,000 for the whistle.
flow.parent: 340 divided by 200 is 1.7 metres for the voice. 340 divided by 3,000 is about 0.11 metres, or 11 centimetres, for the whistle. Notice that the higher sound has the shorter wavelength, just as with ripples. This rule is the same for every wave.

activities.title: Spreading Rings: where does the energy go?
activities.context: In this activity you drop a marble into still water from different heights, and watch the rings spread out and fade.

materials.item: a wide, shallow bowl, tray or steel thali with a rim (the bigger, the better), filled with water about 2 centimetres deep
a marble, or a small steel nut or pebble
a ruler to measure the drop height
a dark cloth or dark paper under the bowl, so the rings show up
a torch to shine from the side, and a phone to film in slow motion, if you have one

activities.safety: Keep marbles and small nuts away from younger children, because they can be swallowed. Wipe up any splashed water at once, because a wet floor is slippery.

schedule.what: Drop a marble from 5, 20 and 40 centimetres. Watch how tall the first ring is and how far it spreads before it fades.

activities.record: Draw the rings for each drop height. Mark where each ring seemed to fade away.

flow.do: Put the bowl on a dark cloth on a flat table. Let the water go still. Ask your child to guess what will happen to a ring as it spreads, and why.
flow.say: A marble will make a ring of ripples. As the ring spreads out, will it get taller, lower or stay the same? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Drop a marble. Will the ring get taller, lower or stay the same? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think the ring will change as it spreads?
good: It will get lower, because it runs out of push.
It will stay the same, because nothing takes it away.
It will get lower because it spreads out.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Write it down.
flow.context: This is the first step of Spreading Rings. You guess before you drop the marble.

flow.do: Hold the marble 20 centimetres above the middle of the water. Let it go. Watch the ring spread, and count how many rings you can see. Lay a ruler beside the bowl and note how far from the splash the last ring can still be seen. Draw it. Then drop from 5 centimetres and from 40 centimetres, and do the same. Repeat each height twice.
flow.say: Drop the marble from 20 centimetres and watch the first ring closely. Then drop from 5 centimetres, and from 40. What changes about the ring?
flow.kid: Drop from 20 centimetres. Watch the ring. Then drop from 5 and 40.
flow.parent: A higher drop gives a taller ring that spreads further before it fades. Every ring gets lower as it spreads. If the dark cloth under a clear bowl is not enough, shine a torch from the side. Wipe up any splashes. In a small thali the ring reaches the rim in under a second and bounces back, which muddles the result; a big tray or the Tap Faster tray is better. Shine a torch from the side in a dim room. A phone slow-motion video helps a lot. With 2 to 4 children: one drops, one holds the ruler and torch, one films, one draws and counts.

check.q: A ring of ripples spreads out and gets lower. What is most likely happening to the wave's energy?
options: It is shared out over a longer and longer ring, so each part has less
It is being used up by the marble
It is being pushed back into the middle
check.why: The same energy is spread over a ring that grows longer all the time, so each little piece of it has less, and the ring is lower. A small part also turns into a tiny amount of heat. If you picked the marble, remember that it stopped on the bottom as soon as the ring left.

flow.context: In this step, you drop the marble from three heights and draw the rings.

flow.do: Compare your three drawings. Ask which ring was tallest at the start, and which went furthest before fading.
flow.say: Look at your three drawings. Which drop made the tallest first ring? Which ring went the furthest? What does the height tell you about the energy?
flow.kid: Compare the drawings. Which ring was tallest? Which went furthest?
flow.think: A higher drop gave a taller ring. What do you think that tells us about the energy it carried?
flow.parent: A higher drop gives the marble more energy, and the tall ring carries more of it. Amplitude is the height of a wave above its rest level, and it tells you the energy of the wave.

activities.title: Tiny Taps, Big Swing: pushing a pendulum at the right time
activities.context: In this activity you tap a hanging washer with a finger, first at its own beat and then at the wrong beat, and see which makes the swing grow.

materials.item: the pendulum from Counting Swings: a washer on a 50 centimetre thread
a door frame or window grill to hang it from
a phone with a stopwatch
a chair to sit on beside the pendulum
a phone with a free metronome app, set to 60 beats a minute
a ruler to measure how wide the swing is

activities.safety: Stand to the side of the swing, and tap with a fingertip, never with a hard object, so the washer does not fly off. Switch the fan off, because moving air spoils the swing.

schedule.what: Tap a hanging washer once for each swing, then at the wrong beat. See which one makes the swing grow.

activities.record: Write 'tapped at its beat' and 'tapped at the wrong beat'. Under each, write what the swing did.

flow.do: Hang the pendulum so it is still. Ask your child to guess whether many small taps will make a big swing, and whether it matters when they tap.
flow.say: We have a still pendulum. We will tap it with one finger, very lightly. If we tap it many times, will it swing wide? Does it matter when we tap? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Tap the still washer many times. Will it swing wide? Does timing matter? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think the timing of the taps matters, or does not matter?
good: Tapping at the right moment is like pushing a swing.
Taps add up whenever you do them.
Tapping at the wrong time will stop it.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. A pendulum 50 centimetres long swings once about every 1.4 seconds.
flow.context: This is the first step of Tiny Taps, Big Swing. You guess before you tap.

flow.do: Start the washer swinging a little. Each time it swings back to you, give it a very light tap with one fingertip, in the direction it is going. Tap for about 20 swings. Watch the size of the swing.
flow.say: Wait until the washer is coming toward your finger. Give it a gentle tap, in the direction it is going. Do it once for each swing. Keep going for about 20 swings. What happens to the swing?
flow.kid: Tap the washer as it comes toward you. Tap once each swing. Watch.
flow.parent: The swing should grow clearly, from a few centimetres to a very wide swing. Each tap is tiny, but taps at the same beat add up. If it does not grow, the taps are probably arriving as the washer moves away. Wait, and feel the beat first. Tap once each full swing, when the washer is coming toward you. After 10 taps and after 20 taps, hold a ruler behind it and note how wide the swing is. A thread can start to twist the washer in a circle; if it does, stop and let it go still.

check.q: Why did very light taps make the swing grow wide?
options: Each tap came at the same moment in every swing, so the taps added up
Each tap was a very hard push
The washer was pushed harder because of its weight
check.why: The taps were light but they arrived at the beat of the pendulum, so each one added to the swing already there. A single light tap alone does little. If you picked a hard push, remember that you tapped very lightly.

flow.context: In this step, you tap at the pendulum's own beat and watch the swing grow.

flow.do: Let the swing settle. Switch on the metronome at 60 beats a minute. Tap the washer on every click, even when it is not coming toward you. Tap for 20 taps. Measure how wide the swing is after 10 and after 20 taps, and compare with before.
flow.say: Now tap once every second, whatever the washer is doing. That is not its beat. Watch what the swing does. Is it as big as before?
flow.kid: Tap once every second, whatever the washer does. Is the swing as big?
flow.parent: The swing will swell a little and shrink again, and stay much smaller than before, because the taps drift in and out of step with the washer (it swings about every 1.4 seconds and you tap every 1 second). Your numbers will vary, so compare the widest swing with the earlier one. This is why a crowd walking out of step does not make a bridge swing, but a crowd stepping in time with it can. With 2 to 4 children, take turns tapping while the others measure.
flow.think: What would you have to do to make the pendulum swing wide at a tapping rate of once every second?

projects.title: Ripple Speed Machine: work out how fast ripples travel
projects.context: In this 2-day project you use your tapping rate and the gap between ripples to work out how fast ripples travel, and then find out what depth does to the speed.

materials.item: the tray, ruler, torch, metronome and towels from the Tap Faster test
a phone camera, to photograph the ripples from above (the grown-up's phone is fine)
a calculator, or pencil and paper
graph paper or squared paper for a line graph
a jug or mug to pour the water, and a ruler to check the depth

projects.safety: Wipe up spilt water straight away, because it makes the floor slippery.

schedule.what: Tap at 2, 3 and 4 taps each second in 1 centimetre of water. Photograph the ripples, measure the gaps, and multiply taps by gap to get the speed.
Tap at 3 taps each second in water 0.5, 1 and 2 centimetres deep. Work out the speed each time, and draw a graph of speed against depth.

projects.record: Day 1: a table of taps each second, gap and speed. Day 2: a table of depth, gap and speed, and a line graph of speed against depth.

flow.do: Set up the tray with water 1 centimetre deep, as in Tap Faster. Lay a ruler along the edge of the tray so it shows in the photos. Tap at 2 taps each second and take a photo from above.
flow.say: We will use the rule that speed is the taps each second times the gap between ripples. Set up the tray as before. Lay a ruler along the edge so the photo shows the scale.
flow.kid: Set up the tray. Lay a ruler along the edge. Tap and take a photo.
flow.parent: Hold the phone steady and as straight above the tray as you can. If the photo does not show the bright lines, shine the torch from another angle. A video clip works too: pause on a sharp frame. Lay the ruler on the paper under the tray, along the way the ripples travel, so that it lines up with the lines and there is no sideways error from the camera. With 2 to 4 children: one taps, one keeps the metronome, one photographs, one measures and writes. Switch the fan off.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Ripple Speed Machine. You set up the tray and take a photo at 2 taps each second.

flow.do: Repeat at 3 and 4 taps each second. Look at the photos. Measure the gap between the bright lines using the ruler in the photo. Write each gap in a table.
flow.say: Now photograph the ripples at 3 taps and at 4 taps each second. Then look at the photos and measure the gaps against the ruler. Write them in the table.
flow.kid: Take photos at 3 taps and 4 taps. Measure the gaps from the photos.
flow.parent: Expect gaps of about 14, 10 and 7 centimetres for 2, 3 and 4 taps each second. If a gap is more than 1 or 2 centimetres from this, measure again.

check.q: At 3 taps each second, the gap between ripples is 10 centimetres. How fast are the ripples travelling?
check.why: Speed is taps each second times the gap. 3 times 10 is 30 centimetres each second. Adding 3 and 10 to get 13 is a common slip. The speed rule is a product, not a sum.

flow.context: In this step, you photograph ripples at three tap rates and measure the gaps.

flow.do: Multiply taps each second by the gap for each row. Write the speed. Look at the three speeds. Ask your child whether they are close to each other, and why.
flow.say: Multiply the taps each second by the gap in every row. You get a speed in centimetres each second. Look at the three answers. Are they close to each other? Why might that be?
flow.kid: Multiply taps each second by the gap. Are the three speeds close?
flow.parent: The three speeds should be close, around 25 to 35 centimetres each second, though yours may differ a little. They are close because the water, and not the tapping, sets the speed. Small differences come from measuring error.
flow.context: In this step, you work out the speed from each row and compare them.

flow.do: Make a prediction. At 3 taps each second, will the gap be longer, shorter or the same if the water is deeper? Write the guess and the reason down.
flow.say: Last time we changed the taps. Today we change the depth of the water, and keep the taps at 3 each second. In deeper water, will the gap between ripples be longer, shorter or the same? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Deeper water, same taps. Will the gap be longer, shorter or the same? Why?
flow.parent: In the Class 3 Tray Test, ripples went faster in deeper water. If they go faster, and the taps are the same, the gap must grow. Let your child work out this link before you say it.
flow.context: On day 2, you guess what depth will do to the gap, before you test.

flow.do: Make the water 0.5 centimetres, 1 centimetre and 2 centimetres deep in turn. Tap at 3 taps each second. Take a photo at each depth. Measure the gap. Work out the speed.
flow.say: Measure the water carefully each time. Tap at 3 taps each second, take a photo, and measure the gap. Then multiply by 3 to get the speed in centimetres each second.
flow.kid: Try three depths. Tap at 3 each second. Photo, measure, then multiply.
flow.parent: Expect gaps of about 7, 10 and 13 centimetres, so speeds of about 21, 30 and 39. The speed grows as the water gets deeper, but not in a straight line. Shallow ripples travel in a different way from deep ones. Your numbers will not be exact, so look for the pattern. Depth is the hard part. Check it with a ruler at all four corners, because a tilt of 1 millimetre is a big share of 0.5 centimetres. For 0.5 centimetres dip the ruler only about 2 millimetres. About 0.5 litre fills a 35 by 25 centimetre tray to 0.5 centimetres, 1 litre to 1 centimetre and 2 litres to 2 centimetres. If your three speeds do not rise neatly, trust the trend between the shallowest and the deepest. These numbers are typical, not promised.
flow.context: On day 2, you measure the gap at three depths and work out the speed.

flow.do: Draw a line graph. Put depth along the bottom and speed up the side. Plot the three points and join them. Ask your child what the graph shows.
flow.say: Draw a graph with depth along the bottom and speed up the side. Put a dot for each depth and join the dots. What does the line do as the water gets deeper?
flow.kid: Draw the graph. Depth along the bottom. Speed up the side. Join the dots.

check.q: In your graph, the line rises as the depth increases. What does this say about ripples?
options: Ripples travel faster in deeper water
Ripples travel slower in deeper water
Ripples travel at the same speed in all depths
check.why: The line goes up as the water gets deeper, so the speed grows. This matches what you found in the Class 3 Tray Test. If you chose slower, check which axis is speed and which is depth.

flow.context: On day 2, you draw a line graph of speed against depth.

setup.caption: 1. Tap at a steady rate and photograph the ripples with a ruler in view.

setup.art: A photo of ripples on a phone screen with a child holding a ruler against the screen to measure the gap.
setup.caption: 2. Measure the gap between bright lines. Multiply by the taps each second.

setup.art: Three trays side by side with water 0.5, 1 and 2 centimetres deep and ripples with wider gaps in the deeper trays.
setup.caption: 3. On day 2, change the depth and keep the taps the same.

setup.caption: 4. Draw a graph of speed against depth.

challenges.title: The Thirty-Second Pendulum: build a timer from a thread
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. You build a pendulum that counts thirty seconds for you, without looking at a clock.
challenges.safety: A grown-up fixes the thread high up. Hang it where nobody walks past and nothing breakable is near, and stand to the side of the swing, because a steel washer that hits a face can hurt.
challenges.problem: Build a pendulum that makes exactly 30 swings in 30 seconds, give or take one second. It must do this twice in a row. Then use it to time 30 seconds of something fun.
constraints: Use only thread, a washer or nut, tape and a measuring tape. No stopwatch while building, only to test.
The pendulum must hang free and swing in a straight line, without touching anything.
Release the washer without pushing it. The swing must be small, under 15 centimetres to the side.
It must pass the test twice in a row, with 30 swings in between 29 and 31 seconds.
materials: a strong cotton thread about 1 metre long
a phone stopwatch to check your result
a door frame or window grill to hang the pendulum from
general: Use what you learned in Counting Swings: the 25 centimetre pendulum swung about once each second. Start at 25 centimetres and adjust.
Test 30 swings each time, then lengthen or shorten the thread by a centimetre and test again.
creative: Make a metronome from a ruler hung from a pin: tape a weight near the bottom, and slide it up or down the ruler to change the beat.
Build a pendulum that swings once every two seconds, and then work out how long the thread must be, by changing it from the 25 centimetre one.
challenges.your_turn: Sketch your pendulum. Predict the length you need. Build it and test it. If 30 swings take more than 30 seconds, make the thread shorter. If less, make it longer. How close can you get?

setup.art: A child sketching a pendulum with a length arrow and a guess of 25 centimetres written beside it.
setup.caption: 1. Plan your pendulum and guess the length you need.

setup.art: A pendulum hanging in a door frame with a stopwatch beside it showing 30 seconds and a child counting aloud.
setup.caption: 2. Test 30 swings against the stopwatch.

setup.art: A hand shortening the thread by a centimetre, with the old and new lengths marked.
setup.caption: 3. Adjust the thread a centimetre at a time until it passes twice.

flow.do: Read the problem together. Look at the results from Counting Swings. Ask your child to guess the length and draw a sketch.
flow.say: We need 30 swings in 30 seconds. That is one swing each second. Which length gave about one swing each second in Counting Swings? Draw your pendulum and write your guess.
flow.kid: You need one swing each second. Which length was that? Draw your plan.

ask.q: What length do you think you will need?
good: About 25 centimetres, like the shortest in the test.
Something near 25 centimetres, but I will check.
I do not know, so I will test a few.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Thirty-Second Pendulum. You plan.

flow.do: Hang a washer on a thread at your guessed length. Time 30 swings with the stopwatch. Write the time. Is it more or less than 30 seconds?
flow.say: Build your first pendulum. Time 30 swings. Write down the time, so you have something to improve.
flow.kid: Build your pendulum. Time 30 swings. Write the time.
flow.parent: If your first try is far off, do not worry. A pendulum 25 centimetres long should take about 30 seconds for 30 swings. Count out loud and keep the swing small, because a big swing changes the time a little. If your thread stretches or the knot slips, the length will drift.
flow.context: In this step, you build the first pendulum and test it.

flow.do: Change the length by a centimetre. Time 30 swings again. Keep changing until your pendulum makes 30 swings in 29 to 31 seconds. Write down every length and time.
flow.say: If 30 swings took more than 30 seconds, the pendulum is too slow, so make it shorter. If less, make it longer. Change one centimetre each time.
flow.kid: Too slow? Shorten it. Too fast? Lengthen it. Test again.
flow.parent: A change of 1 centimetre makes a change of about half a second in 30 swings at this length. It is easy to overshoot, so change in small steps. Keep a table of lengths and times to help you.

check.q: Your pendulum takes 33 seconds for 30 swings. What should you do?
check.why: Taking more time means the pendulum is too slow, and a shorter pendulum swings faster. A heavier washer changes nothing, as you saw in the test.

flow.context: In this step, you adjust the length until the pendulum passes the test.

flow.do: Test the pendulum twice in a row. Then use it to time 30 seconds of something fun, such as a dance or a tongue-twister. Ask your child how they know it is accurate.
flow.say: Test your pendulum twice. When it passes, use it to time 30 seconds of something fun. How do you know your timer is right?
flow.kid: Pass the test twice. Then time 30 seconds of something fun.
flow.think: A clock keeps time with a swinging pendulum. Why would a longer or shorter pendulum make the clock run wrong?
flow.parent: Pendulum clocks were the best timekeepers for about 300 years after Christiaan Huygens built the first one in the 1650s. A clock that runs too fast is fixed by lengthening its pendulum, and one that runs too slow is fixed by shortening it.

items.p: A pendulum makes 10 swings in 20 seconds. How many swings does it make each second?
items.why: 10 swings in 20 seconds is 10 divided by 20, which is half a swing each second. Its frequency is half a hertz. If you chose 2, you divided the wrong way round.

items.p: The number of times something repeats each second is called its ____.
items.why: Frequency tells you how often. A clock that ticks once a second has a frequency of one hertz.

items.p: Three pendulums hang side by side. One has a 20 centimetre thread, one has 50 and one has 100. Which one swings most often?
opts: The one with the 20 centimetre thread
The one with the 50 centimetre thread
The one with the 100 centimetre thread
items.why: A shorter pendulum swings more often. Length is the thing that sets a pendulum's beat.

items.p: If you hang a heavier washer on the same thread, the pendulum swings faster.
items.why: False. The time of a swing depends on the length, not the weight. A heavier washer is pulled down harder but is also harder to move, and these cancel.

items.p: Three of these are different ways of saying how often a pendulum swings. Which one is not?
opts: A frequency of half a hertz
A thread that is 100 centimetres long
items.why: The first three all say the same thing about the beat. The length of the thread is a distance, and tells you nothing by itself about how often.

items.p: Match each word to what it means.
items.why: These five words are the tools for talking about any wave.
pairs: how many crests pass a spot each second
the time one full wave takes
the distance from one crest to the next
how far the crest rises above the flat level
how far a crest travels each second

items.p: Is each one set by the source of a wave, or by the material the wave travels through?
items.why: The source decides how often crests are made. The material decides how fast each crest travels.
items: how many taps are made each second
how fast a ripple moves across the water
how fast a dupatta is flicked
how fast a sound moves through air
how often a guitar string shakes

items.p: Ripples travel 20 centimetres each second. You tap twice each second. How far apart are the ripples?
items.why: The gap is the speed divided by the taps each second. 20 divided by 2 is 10 centimetres. Adding 20 and 2 to get 22 is a common slip.

items.p: When the wave speed stays the same, a higher frequency makes a ____ wavelength.
items.why: More crests are made each second, so the same distance holds more of them, and each gap is smaller.

items.p: A wave with a bigger amplitude carries more energy than a wave with a smaller amplitude.
items.why: True. A tall wave has more energy in it. That is why a big sea wave can knock you over and a ripple cannot.

items.p: Which kind of wave is sound in air?
opts: A push wave, where the air is squeezed and spread along the way the sound goes
A shake wave, where the air moves up and down across the way the sound goes
A wave that needs no material to travel through
items.why: Sound in air is a push wave. The air is squeezed together and spread out along the line of travel. Air cannot hold its shape sideways, so it cannot carry a shake wave.

items.p: Put these in order of wavelength, from the shortest to the longest.
a: a sea wave at a beach
items.why: Red light is under a thousandth of a millimetre. A Wi-Fi wave is about 12 centimetres. An FM radio wave is about 3 metres. A sea wave at a beach can be about 100 metres.
items: a sea wave at a beach

items.p: Label the drawing of a wave: crest, trough, wavelength, amplitude.
items.why: The crest is the top, and the trough is the bottom. The wavelength goes from one crest to the next. The amplitude goes from the flat middle line up to the crest.
items.art: A wavy line with a dotted flat line through its middle and four blank label lines pointing to the top, the bottom, a crest-to-crest gap and a flat-line-to-crest gap.

items.p: A friend says that tapping the water faster will make the ripples travel faster. Explain to your friend what really happens.
items.a: Tapping faster makes more ripples each second, but each ripple still travels at the speed the water allows. So the ripples end up closer together. The water sets the speed, and the tapping sets how often.
items.why: A strong answer says the speed stays the same, that the number of ripples each second goes up, and that the gaps shrink.

items.p: Draw a tray with ripples from slow taps on one side and ripples from fast taps on the other. Show the difference in the gaps.
items.a: Two sets of curved or straight lines, with wide gaps for slow taps and narrow gaps for fast taps. A strong drawing shows about half the gap for double the taps.
items.why: A drawing like this shows the key finding: faster taps make closer ripples.
items.art: A blank tray outline, with a left half and a right half to draw in.

items.p: A parent pushes a child on a swing at the moment the swing comes back to her each time. Why does the swing get higher and higher?
opts: Each push comes at the swing's own beat, so each one adds to the swing already there
Each push is harder than the one before
The swing gets lighter as it goes up
items.why: Small pushes at the right moment add up. Pushes at any other moment would partly cancel. Hitting the beat is what matters, not the strength of each push.

items.p: Sound in air travels about 340 metres each second. A note has a frequency of 340 hertz. How long is one wave of the note?
items.why: Wavelength is the speed divided by the frequency. 340 divided by 340 is 1 metre. Multiplying to get 115,600 is the slip of using the wrong operation.

items.p: A second note has a frequency of 680 hertz, twice the first, in the same air. What is its wavelength?
items.why: 340 divided by 680 is half a metre. Doubling the frequency halves the wavelength when the speed stays the same.

items.p: Wave speed equals frequency times ____.
items.why: Each second, a number of waves pass, and each one has a length. Multiply the two and you have the distance the wave travelled in that second.

items.p: Radio waves travel at 300 million metres each second. A station sends 100 million waves each second. How long is each wave?
items.why: 300 million divided by 100 million is 3. Each wave is 3 metres long. Check the zeros carefully: 30 or 0.3 would need a different frequency.

items.p: A pendulum of the same length would swing more slowly on the Moon than on the Earth.
items.why: True. The Moon pulls things down more weakly, so the pendulum is pulled back more gently and takes longer for each swing. A pendulum's beat comes from its length and the pull around it.

items.p: Match each wave to the kind it is.
items.why: Push waves squeeze and stretch the material along the line of travel. Shake waves move it across the line. Light needs no material.
pairs: a wave that crosses empty space

items.p: In a pendulum test, does changing each one change how often the pendulum swings?
items.why: Only the length of the thread changes the beat. Weight, small changes in width and colour do not.
items: how wide the swing is, for small swings

items.p: Put these in order of frequency, from the lowest to the highest.
a: a violin string at concert pitch
items.why: A clock ticks once each second. A bee beats her wings about 200 times each second. A violin string shakes 440 times each second. An FM radio wave has about 100 million each second.
items: a violin string at concert pitch

items.p: Three of these are about how often. Which one is about how far?
items.why: Frequency, hertz and taps each second all count how often. Wavelength is a distance, from one crest to the next.

items.p: A ring of ripples spreads out and gets lower as it grows. Why?
opts: The same energy is spread over a longer ring, so each part has less
The ripples get heavier as they travel
The water at the edge pushes back and flattens them
items.why: A bigger ring is a longer line of water, and the energy of the splash is shared along all of it. Each bit has less, so the wave is lower.

items.p: A radio signal always shows up at the same place among the stars, about four minutes earlier by the clock each day. Where does the signal most likely come from?
opts: From far away among the stars, because it follows the stars' timing
From something on Earth, such as a car or a radio
From the Sun, because the Sun rises every day
items.why: The stars rise about four minutes earlier each day. A signal that keeps their time is following the sky, not anything on the ground.

items.p: A friend says that if you shake the end of a long rope faster, the waves will travel faster along the rope. Is your friend right? Explain.
items.a: No. Shaking faster makes more waves each second, so the waves are closer together, but they travel at the speed that the rope allows. A tighter rope would carry them faster.
items.why: A strong answer says that the speed is set by the rope and not by the shaking, and that shaking faster shortens the wavelength.

items.p: A radio station says it broadcasts at 100 megahertz. Radio waves travel at 300 million metres each second. Explain how you would work out the length of its waves.
items.a: A hundred megahertz means 100 million waves each second. In one second the waves stretch 300 million metres. So each wave is 300 million divided by 100 million, which is 3 metres.
items.why: A strong answer divides the speed by the frequency and gets 3 metres, and says why: the distance in one second is shared among that many waves.

items.p: Asha and Karthik are watching a pendulum swing once every 2 seconds. They argue about where the 2 seconds comes from.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side, gives a reason from the pendulum test, and says what is right in the other view.
items.why: Both have part of the truth. The pendulum swings at its own steady beat. The number 2 and the word second come from a clock and a count that people agreed on.

views.says: The beat is in the pendulum. It swung like that before anyone counted, and it would keep swinging that way if we left.
The 2 seconds is in our counting. Nature has a swinging thing. We made the clock, and the number comes from the clock.

items.ask: Which idea do you agree with most? Give a reason from your pendulum test. Then say one thing the other person has right.

items.p: Label the drawing of a pendulum: pivot, length, bob and one swing.
items.why: The pivot is the fixed point at the top. The length goes from the pivot to the middle of the bob. The bob is the weight at the end. One swing is out and all the way back.
items.art: A pendulum hanging from a door frame with a washer on the end and dotted arcs, and four blank label lines pointing to the top, the thread, the washer and the full arc.

items.p: Draw two waves on the same line, both moving at the same speed. Make one with a higher frequency than the other. Show how their wavelengths differ.
items.a: Two wavy lines, one with crests close together and one with crests far apart. The one with crests close together has the higher frequency and the shorter wavelength.
items.why: A strong drawing shows closer crests for the higher frequency, because the same distance holds more waves.
items.art: Two blank wave strips, one above the other, each with a start line at the left.

items.p: Light needs air to travel through, just as sound does.
items.why: False. Light is a wave that can cross empty space. That is how sunlight reaches us. Sound needs a material, such as air or water.

items.p: A pendulum 1 metre long swings once in 2 seconds. Making it four times as long, 4 metres, makes the time for one swing twice as long. How long must a pendulum be to swing once in 4 seconds?
items.why: Twice the time needs four times the length, as the pattern shows. 1 metre gives 2 seconds, so 4 metres gives 4 seconds. Doubling the length to 2 metres would give a time about 1.4 times longer, not twice.

items.p: Ripples are made 5 times each second and travel 25 centimetres each second. What is the gap between ripples?
items.why: The gap is the speed divided by the frequency. 25 divided by 5 is 5 centimetres. Multiplying gives 125, which is a slip of using the wrong rule.

items.p: The gap between ripples is 4 centimetres, and they are made 6 times each second. How fast do they travel?
items.why: Speed is the frequency times the gap. 6 times 4 is 24 centimetres each second. Dividing gives 1.5, the wrong way round.

items.p: You keep tapping a tray of water at 3 taps each second, and then you pour in more water so it is deeper. What happens to the gap between ripples?
opts: The gap gets longer, because ripples travel faster in deeper water
The gap gets shorter, because deeper water is heavier
The gap stays the same, because the taps are the same
items.why: Ripples go faster in deeper water. The taps are the same, so there are still 3 crests each second, but each crest goes further before the next is made. The gap grows.

items.p: A clock that runs too fast can be fixed by making its pendulum ____.
items.why: A longer pendulum swings more slowly, so each tick takes a bit longer and the clock slows down.

items.p: A star that spins 700 times each second sends a pulse of radio waves about every 1.4 thousandths of a second.
items.why: True. One spin takes 1 divided by 700 seconds, which is about 0.0014 seconds, or 1.4 thousandths of a second. A high frequency means a short period.

items.p: Match each wave to its rough wavelength.
items.why: Wavelength is the speed divided by the frequency. The higher the frequency, the shorter the wave.
pairs: An FM radio wave at 100 megahertz
A sound of 1,000 hertz in air
An AM radio wave at 1 megahertz

items.p: Is each one a push wave or a shake wave?
items.why: In a push wave the material moves along the line of travel. In a shake wave it moves across that line.
items: a squeeze along a spring toy

items.p: Put these steps in order for working out how fast ripples travel.
a: Tap the water at a steady rate you know
Photograph the ripples with a ruler in view
Measure the gap between the bright lines
Multiply the taps each second by the gap
items.why: You need a known tap rate and a measured gap. The speed is their product.
items: Measure the gap between the bright lines
Tap the water at a steady rate you know
Multiply the taps each second by the gap
Photograph the ripples with a ruler in view

items.p: Three of these are examples of pushes arriving at the natural beat. Which is not?
opts: Pushing a child on a swing as she comes back to you
Soldiers marching in step across a flimsy bridge
Tapping a hanging washer once for each swing
Dropping a marble into still water
items.why: A marble dropped once is one push, not a series of pushes timed to a beat. The other three are pushes repeated at the beat of the thing being pushed.

items.p: A telescope picks up pulses of radio waves 1.3 seconds apart from one spot in the sky, year after year. Which explanation fits best?
opts: A spinning star whose beam sweeps past Earth once each spin
A radio on Earth that is switched on at the same time every night
A planet that flashes its light on and off
items.why: A star spinning steadily with a beam, like a lighthouse, gives a very regular beat. A signal made on Earth would not follow the stars' timing.

items.p: Explain why a crowd walking in step can make a footbridge sway wildly, but the same crowd walking out of step cannot.
items.a: A bridge has its own beat, and it swings at that beat. If the people step at the same beat, every push adds to the swing, so it grows. If they walk out of step, some pushes help and some push the other way, so they cancel and the swing stays small.
items.why: A strong answer says that the bridge has its own beat, that pushes at that beat add up, and that pushes at other times cancel.

items.p: Ripples are made 2 times each second, and the gap between them is 15 centimetres. A friend says the ripples travel at 15 centimetres each second. Is the friend right? Show your working.
items.a: No. In one second, 2 ripples are made, each 15 centimetres apart. So the front ripple travels 2 times 15, which is 30 centimetres each second. The friend forgot to multiply by the taps each second.
items.why: A strong answer multiplies the frequency by the gap and gets 30 centimetres each second, and says what the friend forgot.

items.p: Gravitational waves from crashing black holes were first caught in 2015, though the idea is much older. Why might it have taken so long to catch one?
items.a: The waves are extremely small by the time they reach us. The wave is so low that it changes the length of an instrument by far less than the width of a proton. It took very careful, very sensitive instruments to measure that.
items.why: A strong answer says that the amplitude is tiny by the time the wave reaches Earth, and that catching it needed instruments of great sensitivity.

items.p: A young student notices a strange, steady signal that no one expected. Her supervisor explains it and publishes the paper. Later, the supervisor is given the prize.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side, gives a reason based on who noticed, who explained and who has the power, and fairly says what is right in the other view.
items.why: Both views have a point. Noticing the signal was essential and was hers. Explaining it and leading the team also took skill. Real discoveries need both, and who gets credit depends on rules people have agreed, which can be unfair.

views.says: She saw it first and she kept checking it when everyone said it was nothing. The prize should go to her.
The team was built and led by the supervisor, and the paper explained it. A prize is for the whole discovery, which takes both.

items.ask: Which idea do you agree with most? Give a reason. Then say one thing the other person has right.

items.why: Two waves at the same speed: the one with crests close together has more crests each second, so a higher frequency and a shorter wavelength. The other has the lower frequency and the longer wavelength.

quiz.p: Which of these is a frequency?
quiz.why: Frequency is a count of how many times something repeats each second. 12 centimetres is a distance and 5 seconds is a time.

quiz.p: A girl hangs a heavy stone and a light stone on two threads of exactly the same length. She lets them both swing a short way. What happens?
opts: They swing together, one swing taking the same time for each
quiz.why: The weight does not change the time of a swing. Only the length does. A heavier stone is pulled down harder but is harder to move.

quiz.p: A finger that taps the water faster makes ripples that travel faster across the water.
quiz.why: False. Faster taps make more ripples each second, so they are closer together. They all travel at the speed the water allows.

quiz.p: Ripples travel 30 centimetres each second. You tap 3 times each second. How far apart are the ripples?
quiz.why: The gap is the speed divided by the frequency. 30 divided by 3 is 10 centimetres.

quiz.p: A bump moves along a rope while the rope moves up and down. How does the rope move in a push wave instead?
opts: Back and forth along the way the wave travels
Up and down across the way the wave travels
Round in a circle, never along
quiz.why: In a push wave the material is squeezed and spread along the line of travel. Sound in air is a push wave.

quiz.p: Two waves on the same string have the same frequency. One is twice as tall as the other. Which carries more energy?
quiz.why: A bigger amplitude means more energy. The frequency is the same, so how tall is the thing that differs.

quiz.p: Red light has a ____ wavelength than violet light.
quiz.why: Red light is about 700 nanometres. Violet is about 400. Red waves are the longest we can see.

quiz.p: A radio station sends 100 million waves each second. Radio waves travel 300 million metres each second. How long is each wave?
quiz.why: 300 million divided by 100 million is 3 metres.

quiz.p: Pulling a pendulum back a little further before letting go makes each of its swings take noticeably longer.
quiz.why: False. For modest swings, the time of one swing stays the same. A wider swing goes further, but it also moves faster.

quiz.p: Why do many small pushes make a swing go very high when each push arrives at the swing's own beat?
opts: Each push adds to the swing that is already there
Each push gets stronger as the swing goes higher
The swing makes the pushes bigger
quiz.why: When a push comes at the right moment, it moves with the swing, so it adds. Pushes at the wrong moment partly cancel.

quiz.p: Which has the longest wavelength: red light, a Wi-Fi wave or an FM radio wave?
quiz.why: An FM radio wave is about 3 metres. A Wi-Fi wave is about 12 centimetres. Red light is under a thousandth of a millimetre.

quiz.p: In an earthquake, which kind of wave cannot travel through the liquid part of the Earth?
quiz.why: A liquid does not hold its shape sideways, so it cannot carry a shake wave. Push waves can cross liquid.

applications: Pendulum clocks and metronomes keep time by the steady beat of a swinging weight, and engineers set the beat by choosing the length.
Radio, television, phones and Wi-Fi each use their own frequency, so many stations can share the air without mixing.
Engineers work out the natural beats of bridges and tall buildings, and fit dampers that soak up the swing, as was done to the Millennium Bridge in London.
Seismologists use the arrival times of P waves and S waves to find where an earthquake began and what the inside of the Earth is like.
Ultrasound scans use sound waves far above the range of human hearing to look inside the body, for example at a baby in the womb.
A microwave oven uses waves about 12 centimetres long, which shake the water in food and warm it.
Musicians tune a tanpura, a violin or a sitar by changing the frequency of each string, using its length and tightness.
Astronomers use some pulsars as clocks in space, and radio telescopes such as the Giant Metrewave Radio Telescope near Pune listen for their beats.
Doctors measure the heartbeat and the breathing rate as frequencies, and watch for changes.
Instruments such as LIGO catch gravitational waves, giving a new way to learn about black holes that give out no light.

open_questions.q: Is there a hum of very slow gravitational waves filling the whole universe?
open_questions.why_open: In 2023, teams around the world, including Indian astronomers who used the Giant Metrewave Radio Telescope near Pune, reported signs of such a hum in the timing of pulsars. Many think it comes from pairs of giant black holes, but this is not settled.

open_questions.q: What is inside a neutron star, the kind of star that becomes a pulsar?
open_questions.why_open: A neutron star is crushed more tightly than anything on Earth, and no experiment can copy it. Scientists have ideas about what is inside, but nobody is sure.

open_questions.q: Is there a smallest possible wavelength?
open_questions.why_open: Some physicists think there may be a smallest length in nature, but no experiment has shown it yet, and the ideas that predict it have not been tested.

open_questions.q: Why do groups of fireflies, or people on a bridge, fall into step without meaning to?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists know that small pushes between neighbours can lock their beats together, and they have models of it. Exactly how it happens in each case, and when it starts, is still being worked out.

open_questions.q: Why do some animals, such as bats and moths, tune themselves so well to each other's frequencies?
open_questions.why_open: Bats send out calls and some moths hear them and dodge. Scientists have found many such pairs, but how each pair came to fit each other is still being studied.

open_questions.q: What is a wave in the deepest sense: a thing, or a pattern in something?
open_questions.why_open: Physicists agree on how to calculate every wave. They do not agree on what a wave of light or a wave of matter is, and so philosophers and physicists still argue about it.

maths.problem: In Counting Swings, a 50 centimetre pendulum took 14 seconds for 10 swings. How long did one swing take, in seconds?
maths.explain: 14 seconds shared among 10 swings is 14 divided by 10, which is 1.4 seconds for each swing. We time 10 swings and divide, because the stopwatch is then wrong by a tiny part of the answer.
maths.context: In the Counting Swings test, you time 10 swings of a pendulum and want to know the time for one.
maths.why_maths: Timing many swings and dividing gives a more accurate answer than timing one swing, because a late press of the stopwatch matters less.

maths.problem: Aditi counts 22 pulse beats in 15 seconds. How many beats would she count in a whole minute? Is this a count of beats each minute or each second?
maths.answer: 88 beats in a minute, which is a count of beats each minute.
maths.explain: A minute has four lots of 15 seconds. 22 times 4 is 88. We can say it is 88 beats each minute. To get beats each second, we would divide 88 by 60, which is a little under one and a half.
maths.context: In Hertz Hunt, you count your pulse for 15 seconds and turn it into beats each minute.
maths.why_maths: A short count scaled up gives a rate for a whole minute, so you can compare your pulse with any other rate.

maths.problem: In a tray, ripples are made 4 times each second, and the gap between them is 7 centimetres. How fast are the ripples travelling?
maths.explain: Each second, 4 ripples are made, each 7 centimetres behind the one in front. The front ripple travels 4 times 7, which is 28 centimetres in one second.
maths.context: In Tap Faster, you tap the water and measure the gap between ripples.
maths.why_maths: Multiplying the taps by the gap turns two things you can measure into a speed you cannot easily time.

maths.problem: Sound in air travels about 340 metres each second. A bass drum makes a sound of 85 hertz. How long is one wave of the sound?
maths.explain: The wavelength is the speed divided by the frequency. 340 divided by 85 is 4. So each wave of the drum is 4 metres long. That is longer than a car.
maths.context: In the Wavelength Ladder, you use speed divided by frequency to find the length of a wave.
maths.why_maths: Dividing speed by frequency lets you predict the length of a wave without being able to see it.

maths.problem: At 2 taps each second the ripples are 14 centimetres apart. Without testing, what gap would you expect at 4 taps each second, and why?
maths.explain: Doubling the taps doubles the ripples made each second, and the speed stays the same. So the same stretch holds twice as many, and each gap is half as big. Half of 14 is 7.
maths.context: In Tap Faster, the gap between ripples shrinks when you tap faster.
maths.why_maths: Thinking about ratios lets you predict a result before you test it, and then check if you were right.

maths.problem: A 25 centimetre pendulum swings once in 1 second. A 100 centimetre one swings once in 2 seconds. Using the pattern, how long would a pendulum need to be to swing once in 3 seconds?
maths.explain: 1 second needs 25 centimetres, which is 25 times 1 times 1. 2 seconds needs 100, which is 25 times 2 times 2. So 3 seconds needs 25 times 3 times 3, which is 225 centimetres.
maths.context: In Counting Swings, a pendulum four times as long takes twice as long for one swing.
maths.why_maths: Spotting the pattern between length and time lets you predict a pendulum you have not built.

maths.problem: The fastest known pulsar spins about 700 times each second. About how many times does it spin in one minute? Round to the nearest thousand.
maths.explain: A minute has 60 seconds. 700 times 60 is 42,000. The pulsar spins about 42,000 times in a minute.
maths.context: In the pulsars card, some neutron stars spin hundreds of times each second.
maths.why_maths: Multiplying a rate by the time shows how big the numbers in the sky really are.

maths.problem: A hair is about 70,000 nanometres wide. A wave of red light is about 700 nanometres long. About how many red light waves would fit across the width of a hair?
maths.explain: 70,000 divided by 700 is 100. So about a hundred red waves would fit across one hair.
maths.context: In the Rainbow from a CD activity, red light waves are about 700 nanometres long.
maths.why_maths: Dividing a big length by a tiny length shows how very small light waves are.

maths.problem: In Tap Faster, a girl measured gaps of 14, 10 and 7 centimetres at 2, 3 and 4 taps each second. She plots these on a line graph with taps along the bottom and gap up the side. About what gap would you expect at 3.5 taps each second?
maths.explain: At 3 taps the gap is 10 and at 4 taps it is 7. 3.5 is half way between, so the gap should be about half way between 10 and 7, which is 8.5 centimetres.
maths.context: After the Tap Faster test, you plot the gaps on a line graph.
maths.why_maths: A line graph lets you read an answer between two measurements without doing another test.

maths.problem: A seconds pendulum swings once every 2 seconds, back and forth. How many full swings does it make in one hour?
maths.explain: One hour is 60 minutes, which is 3,600 seconds. One swing takes 2 seconds, so 3,600 divided by 2 is 1,800 swings.
maths.context: A pendulum with a 100 centimetre thread swings once every 2 seconds, as found in Counting Swings.
maths.why_maths: Changing hours to seconds and dividing shows how many beats a pendulum clock counts in a day.

playtest: Read as a parent and child in a city flat would use it, but not yet tried at home. Counting Swings: a washer on a thread from a door frame, timing 10 swings. The times of about 10, 14 and 20 seconds for 25, 50 and 100 centimetres come from the pendulum rule, and real strings add a second or so of error, so the table says the middle of two tries. The weight and width tests will show differences of under half a second, which is the point. A grown-up must fix the thread high. Tap Faster: this is the most delicate test. Ripples in 1 centimetre of water at 2 to 4 taps each second are 7 to 15 centimetres apart by calculation, and the gap is measured from three bright lines in a 35 centimetre tray. Seeing the lines needs a dim room and a torch from the side, and a towel at the far end stops the ripples bouncing back. If the lines cannot be seen, a phone video played slowly helps. The metronome needs a free app, and a parent clapping the beat also works. The Ripple Speed Machine depends on the same set-up, and its day 2 depth results will be rougher. The speeds of 25 to 35 centimetres each second are calculated, not measured at home, so a family may get different numbers. Facts to check before use: the 1583 lamp story is a reported story, and the details of the Bell pulsar discovery are from her own written account. The wavelength and frequency values on the Faster or Slower cards and in the Wavelength Ladder are rounded and checked by calculation.
